The Reebok Nano X5 cross training shoe made it into our line-up for being the best in the Nano series yet. It steers away from the more aggressive Nano X4 design and toward a shoe we’d choose for lifting and HIIT.

#3323. How The ‘Married At First Sight UK’ Scandal Has Impacted Hit Show Around The World

EXCLUSIVE: The team behind Married at First Sight (MAFS) Australia is “reviewing” Channel 4’s report into the show, which has been axed in the UK following rape allegations.

Deadline asked some of the teams behind versions of MAFS around the world whether they will take heed of the report. Australian broadcaster Channel Nine and MAFS producer Endemol Shine Australia told us they are “examining the findings,” while noting “many of the recommendations for improvement are already in place for MAFS Australia.”

“We are always reviewing our participant protocols to ensure our participants’ safety and wellbeing,” added a spokeswoman for Endemol Shine Australia. “Production of MAFS Australia continues.” Related Stories News Channel 4 Cancels 'Married At First Sight UK' After Rape Allegations News Matthew Weiner Exits Eddie Murphy Peacock Series 'The Chairman' As Showrunner

Channel 4 axed MAFS UK following rape allegations revealed earlier this year by BBC News, which the men accused of wrongdoing deny. Following these allegations being made public, two reviews were commissioned by Channel 4 CEO Priya Dogra, one examining welfare protocols and the other looking into whether changes should be made to protocols to strengthen contributor welfare in the future. While the latter, penned by ex-BBC One boss Lorraine Heggessey, suggested MAFS UK could continue if it took in some changes, Dogra axed the show last week. Watch on Deadline

Many of the versions around the world are made by different production outfits than MAFS UK such as MAFS Australia, which is produced by Banijay-owned Endemol Shine Australia while the UK version is overseen by Seven.One Studios-owned CPL. The two versions are “separate productions and separate shows,” according to the Endemol Shine Australia spokeswoman.

Deadline understands MAFS Australia protocols already in place that were suggested by Heggessey include cast being allowed to keep in touch with friends and family outside the show, a regular refresh of the show’s psychologists, and keeping casting and welfare teams separate.

The Australia team have separate issues they are dealing with. New South Wales Police told BBC News last month that inquiries had taken place “following a report of inappropriate content being shared.” Channel Nine has confirmed that it is “aware of a police investigation.” There were also allegations, published by BBC News, that contestants were not told about their on-screen partners’ previous criminal convictions. Responding in a joint statement, Channel Nine and Endemol Shine Australia said they had “strong protocols in place to ensure participant safety and wellbeing.”

In the U.S., MAFS is made by another different company, North Road-owned Kinetic Content. A spokeswoman declined comment on the Channel 4 review and whether MAFS could implement some of the recommendations in the States. We understand the American version is not currently filming and hasn’t been picked up for new seasons at this point.

MAFS is one of the world’s most successful formats. It originated in Denmark, where it still airs on local network DR1, produced by Seven.One-owned Snowman Productions.

Seven.One told us other versions around the world that it controls remain business as usual, while its distribution arm will continue selling older editions of MAFS UK to global buyers.

A Seven.One spokeswoman said: “The external reviews of contributor welfare on Married at First Sight UK confirmed that Channel 4 and production company CPL’s welfare protocols were compliant with the Ofcom Broadcasting Code; the Heggessey review found that they were ‘extensive, extremely thorough and of a high standard from which other productions in the industry have learnt’. Despite the findings of the reviews, Channel 4 has made the independent strategic decision not to continue the show. This decision has no impact on the show in other countries.”

In the UK, however, the fallout from the cancelation continues. Its axing came on the day Russell Brand, a former Channel 4 presenter, was found guilty of rape and sexual assault. Several days later, allegations of sexually exploitative behavior towards women and teenagers were published about Little Britain co-creator David Walliams, who denies the allegations and says “I am not a sexual predator… I have not broken the law.”

Channel 4 is moving on from MAFS. All past seasons of MAFS UK plus the American, Australian and New Zealand versions have been removed from Channel 4’s VoD platform, while a planned spin-off has been cancelled.

Channel 4 boss Dogra was merely a few weeks into the job when the MAFS UK allegations broke. She will likely face questions on the show when she appears in front of a parliamentary committee on Tuesday and has said its “considerable budget” will now be used to “find the next generation of distinctive and disruptive British television.” This will be a key task for new programs chief David Brindley, who starts in a few weeks’ time.

#3321. 10 Hacks Every Waze User Should Know

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

Waze is a crowdsourced navigation app designed to help you get where you're going as quickly and with as much information about your route as possible. Where Google Maps and Apple Maps offer relatively straightforward directions, Waze tries to outsmart these alternatives by integrating real-time community feedback about hazards, speed traps, road closures, and more. If you are switching to Waze or using it alongside your other navigation tools, these are the hacks to help you maximize everything the app has to offer.

If you find yourself losing track of time or running late for events, Waze can notify you when it's time to leave—based on your current location and live traffic—so you arrive on schedule. You can set up "Time to leave" reminders in advance for individual planned drives, or you can sync your calendar to receive notifications for scheduled events. Calendar sync connects to your device's default calendar app, but you can change this to a third-party alternative if you prefer. Calendar events must include a navigable address to trigger reminders, and you must select Plan a drive in Waze for the event.

Waze has a feature called "child reminders," which are notifications to check for children before you get out of the car. This is clearly an incredibly important use case, but you can also use these alerts for custom messages, like "Don't forget the groceries!" In Waze, tap the menu button > Settings > Reminders > Child reminder and select Custom message.

Variable speed limits, especially on unfamiliar routes, can result in you speeding when you don't mean to. But Waze can alert you if you exceed a customized speed threshold so you aren't caught by surprise or at higher risk of being ticketed. From the menu, go to Settings > Speedometer and turn on Show speedometer. Tap Speeding threshold to select what limit you want to trigger alerts, and turn on Alert at threshold if you want Waze to play a sound.

Waze offers a wealth of information on routes to help drivers navigate obstacles and hazards, but this can clutter your map and distract you from the most critical information, especially in congested, high-traffic areas. Waze says it limits and prioritizes alerts automatically, but you can actually customize which alerts you see based on what's most important to you. From the menu, go to Settings > Alerts and reports > Reports and select the relevant alerts.

In the same Alerts and reports menu, you can enable Alert while driving, which will give you an audio warning and an onscreen pop-up about your selected hazards. This allows you to run navigation via a different map app (like Google Maps or Apple Maps) in the foreground while still getting Waze data in the background.

Waze integrates with toll road and HOV lane passes, so if you have an express or fast lane subscription, your route will optimize for it. If you don't, Waze can still account for HOV lane eligibility if you tell it how many passengers are in your car. From the menu, go to Settings > Toll and HOV passes and tap the plus icon to add your pass(es) from the list. If you need to add your passenger count instead, you can do so from View routes and enable the HOV option.

If you're driving through an unfamiliar, highly congested, or poorly designed area, you can ask Waze to help you avoid tricky maneuvers, such as crossing multiple lanes of traffic or turning left at intersections without lights. This prioritizes ease over speed using protected green arrows, roundabouts, and right turns. From the menu, go to Settings > Navigation, Avoid difficult intersections and select Always. You can also ask Waze to avoid toll roads, ferries, freeways, and unpaved roads.

Waze has a built-in audio player that syncs with your preferred listening platform—such as Spotify, YouTube Music, and Pandora—so you can control your music without having to navigate between apps. (As Waze is a Google product, Apple Music isn't included.) Simply tap the music icon on the map to select your audio player and hit Accept. If you don't see the icon, go to Settings > Audio player and turn on Show on the map.

If you want to make audio directions more interesting, you can select a celebrity or character voice to help you navigate. Recent appearances include Bill Hader's Cat in the Hat and Ziggy Marley. Tap the speaker icon > Current voice to search for the voice or language you want to use. You can also record directions in your own voice.

#3318. Atomically Thin Materials Significantly Shrink Qubits

MIT researchers use 2D materials for capacitors in quantum circuits in an effort to scale processors

Superconducting quantum processor and its microwave packaging.

Quantum computing is a devilishly complex technology, with many technical hurdles impacting its development. Of these challenges two critical issues stand out: miniaturization and qubit quality.

IBM has adopted the superconducting qubit road map of reaching a 1,121-qubit processor by 2023, leading to the expectation that 1,000 qubits with today’s qubit form factor is feasible. However, current approaches will require very large chips (50 millimeters on a side, or larger) at the scale of small wafers, or the use of chiplets on multichip modules. While this approach will work, the aim is to attain a better path toward scalability.

Now researchers at MIT have been able to both reduce the size of the qubits and done so in a way that reduces the interference that occurs between neighboring qubits. The MIT researchers have increased the number of superconducting qubits that can be added onto a device by a factor of 100.

“We are addressing both qubit miniaturization and quality,” said William Oliver, the director for the Center for Quantum Engineering at MIT. “Unlike conventional transistor scaling, where only the number really matters, for qubits, large numbers are not sufficient, they must also be high-performance. Sacrificing performance for qubit number is not a useful trade in quantum computing. They must go hand in hand.”

The key to this big increase in qubit density and reduction of interference comes down to the use of two-dimensional materials, in particular the 2D insulator hexagonal boron nitride (hBN). The MIT researchers demonstrated that a few atomic monolayers of hBN can be stacked to form the insulator in the capacitors of a superconducting qubit.

Just like other capacitors, the capacitors in these superconducting circuits take the form of a sandwich in which an insulator material is sandwiched between two metal plates. The big difference for these capacitors is that the superconducting circuits can operate only at extremely low temperatures—less than 0.02 degrees above absolute zero (-273.15 °C).

Superconducting qubits are measured at temperatures as low as 20 millikelvin in a dilution refrigerator.Nathan Fiske/MIT

In that environment, insulating materials that are available for the job, such as PE-CVD silicon oxide or silicon nitride, have quite a few defects that are too lossy for quantum computing applications. To get around these material shortcomings, most superconducting circuits use what are called coplanar capacitors. In these capacitors, the plates are positioned laterally to one another, rather than on top of one another.

As a result, the intrinsic silicon substrate below the plates and to a smaller degree the vacuum above the plates serve as the capacitor dielectric. Intrinsic silicon is chemically pure and therefore has few defects, and the large size dilutes the electric field at the plate interfaces, all of which leads to a low-loss capacitor. The lateral size of each plate in this open-face design ends up being quite large (typically 100 by 100 micrometers) in order to achieve the required capacitance.

In an effort to move away from the large lateral configuration, the MIT researchers embarked on a search for an insulator that has very few defects and is compatible with superconducting capacitor plates.

“We chose to study hBN because it is the most widely used insulator in 2D material research due to its cleanliness and chemical inertness,” said colead author Joel Wang, a research scientist in the Engineering Quantum Systems group of the MIT Research Laboratory for Electronics.

On either side of the hBN, the MIT researchers used the 2D superconducting material, niobium diselenide. One of the trickiest aspects of fabricating the capacitors was working with the niobium diselenide, which oxidizes in seconds when exposed to air, according to Wang. This necessitates that the assembly of the capacitor occur in a glove box filled with argon gas.

While this would seemingly complicate the scaling up of the production of these capacitors, Wang doesn’t regard this as a limiting factor.

“What determines the quality factor of the capacitor are the two interfaces between the two materials,” said Wang. “Once the sandwich is made, the two interfaces are “sealed” and we don’t see any noticeable degradation over time when exposed to the atmosphere.”

This lack of degradation is because around 90 percent of the electric field is contained within the sandwich structure, so the oxidation of the outer surface of the niobium diselenide does not play a significant role anymore. This ultimately makes the capacitor footprint much smaller, and it accounts for the reduction in cross talk between the neighboring qubits.

“The main challenge for scaling up the fabrication will be the wafer-scale growth of hBN and 2D superconductors like [niobium diselenide], and how one can do wafer-scale stacking of these films,” added Wang.

Wang believes that this research has shown 2D hBN to be a good insulator candidate for superconducting qubits. He says that the groundwork the MIT team has done will serve as a road map for using other hybrid 2D materials to build superconducting circuits.

Dexter Johnson is a contributing editor at IEEE Spectrum, with a focus on nanotechnology.

#3314. How AI Will Change Chip Design

Artificial intelligence’s promise and potential for the semiconductor industry

Rina Diane Caballar is a contributing editor covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment.

An array of semiconductor wafers are ready to be made into chips.

The end of Moore’s Law is looming. Engineers and designers can do only so much to miniaturize transistors and pack as many of them as possible into chips. So they’re turning to other approaches to chip design, incorporating technologies like AI into the process.

Samsung, for instance, is adding AI to its memory chips to enable processing in memory, thereby saving energy and speeding up machine learning. Speaking of speed, Google’s TPU V4 AI chip has doubled its processing power compared with that of its previous version.

But AI holds still more promise and potential for the semiconductor industry. To better understand how AI is set to revolutionize chip design, we spoke with Heather Gorr, senior product manager for MathWorks’ MATLAB platform.

How is AI currently being used to design the next generation of chips?

Heather Gorr: AI is such an important technology because it’s involved in most parts of the cycle, including the design and manufacturing process. There’s a lot of important applications here, even in the general process engineering where we want to optimize things. I think defect detection is a big one at all phases of the process, especially in manufacturing. But even thinking ahead in the design process, [AI now plays a significant role] when you’re designing the light and the sensors and all the different components. There’s a lot of anomaly detection and fault mitigation that you really want to consider.

Then, thinking about the logistical modeling that you see in any industry, there is always planned downtime that you want to mitigate; but you also end up having unplanned downtime. So, looking back at that historical data of when you’ve had those moments where maybe it took a bit longer than expected to manufacture something, you can take a look at all of that data and use AI to try to identify the proximate cause or to see something that might jump out even in the processing and design phases. We think of AI oftentimes as a predictive tool, or as a robot doing something, but a lot of times you get a lot of insight from the data through AI.

What are the benefits of using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Historically, we’ve seen a lot of physics-based modeling, which is a very intensive process. We want to do a reduced order model, where instead of solving such a computationally expensive and extensive model, we can do something a little cheaper. You could create a surrogate model, so to speak, of that physics-based model, use the data, and then do your parameter sweeps, your optimizations, your Monte Carlo simulations using the surrogate model. That takes a lot less time computationally than solving the physics-based equations directly. So, we’re seeing that benefit in many ways, including the efficiency and economy that are the results of iterating quickly on the experiments and the simulations that will really help in the design.

So it’s like having a digital twin in a sense?

Gorr: Exactly. That’s pretty much what people are doing, where you have the physical system model and the experimental data. Then, in conjunction, you have this other model that you could tweak and tune and try different parameters and experiments that let sweep through all of those different situations and come up with a better design in the end.

So, it’s going to be more efficient and, as you said, cheaper?

Gorr: Yeah, definitely. Especially in the experimentation and design phases, where you’re trying different things. That’s obviously going to yield dramatic cost savings if you’re actually manufacturing and producing [the chips]. You want to simulate, test, experiment as much as possible without making something using the actual process engineering.

We’ve talked about the benefits. How about the drawbacks?

Gorr: The [AI-based experimental models] tend to not be as accurate as physics-based models. Of course, that’s why you do many simulations and parameter sweeps. But that’s also the benefit of having that digital twin, where you can keep that in mind—it’s not going to be as accurate as that precise model that we’ve developed over the years.

Both chip design and manufacturing are system intensive; you have to consider every little part. And that can be really challenging. It’s a case where you might have models to predict something and different parts of it, but you still need to bring it all together.

One of the other things to think about too is that you need the data to build the models. You have to incorporate data from all sorts of different sensors and different sorts of teams, and so that heightens the challenge.

How can engineers use AI to better prepare and extract insights from hardware or sensor data?

Gorr: We always think about using AI to predict something or do some robot task, but you can use AI to come up with patterns and pick out things you might not have noticed before on your own. People will use AI when they have high-frequency data coming from many different sensors, and a lot of times it’s useful to explore the frequency domain and things like data synchronization or resampling. Those can be really challenging if you’re not sure where to start.

One of the things I would say is, use the tools that are available. There’s a vast community of people working on these things, and you can find lots of examples [of applications and techniques] on GitHub or MATLAB Central, where people have shared nice examples, even little apps they’ve created. I think many of us are buried in data and just not sure what to do with it, so definitely take advantage of what’s already out there in the community. You can explore and see what makes sense to you, and bring in that balance of domain knowledge and the insight you get from the tools and AI.

What should engineers and designers consider when using AI for chip design?

Gorr: Think through what problems you’re trying to solve or what insights you might hope to find, and try to be clear about that. Consider all of the different components, and document and test each of those different parts. Consider all of the people involved, and explain and hand off in a way that is sensible for the whole team.

How do you think AI will affect chip designers’ jobs?

Gorr: It’s going to free up a lot of human capital for more advanced tasks. We can use AI to reduce waste, to optimize the materials, to optimize the design, but then you still have that human involved whenever it comes to decision-making. I think it’s a great example of people and technology working hand in hand. It’s also an industry where all people involved—even on the manufacturing floor—need to have some level of understanding of what’s happening, so this is a great industry for advancing AI because of how we test things and how we think about them before we put them on the chip.

How do you envision the future of AI and chip design?

Gorr: It’s very much dependent on that human element—involving people in the process and having that interpretable model. We can do many things with the mathematical minutiae of modeling, but it comes down to how people are using it, how everybody in the process is understanding and applying it. Communication and involvement of people of all skill levels in the process are going to be really important. We’re going to see less of those superprecise predictions and more transparency of information, sharing, and that digital twin—not only using AI but also using our human knowledge and all of the work that many people have done over the years.

Rina Diane Caballar is a writer covering tech and its intersections with science, society, and the environment. An IEEE Spectrum contributing editor, she's a former software engineer based in New Zealand.

#3311. Ring's New $250 Indoor Camera Drone Sounds Terrifying

Ring made its name with its smart doorbells with built-in cameras, and now sells more indoor cameras than any other company, capturing more than 40% of the market. When you've already moved tens of millions of devices (enough to raise serious concerns about their use as part of the surveillance state), you always need to keep innovating, and today, the company announced a product it has been working on for a decade: an indoor camera drone powered by artificial intelligence. I got a chance to check it out during a media event yesterday, and I can report that, as harbingers of our dystopian future go, it is only mildly terrifying.

The drone camera is one of two products in the company's new Ring Robotics line, alongside a "rover cam" that looks kind of like the canister of a vacuum cleaner attached to an iPad. While the Ring Rover Cam is priced at $999.99 and targeted at businesses, the Ring Drone Cam is a much more affordable $249.99, reasonable enough that it will appeal to consumers looking for another way to keep (robot) eyes on their stuff.

The drone camera records 2K video and has a 148-degree field of view and the ability to rotate 360 degrees. It works with existing Ring cameras, doorbells, sensors, and alarms, as well as the Alexa Home Map. It has a flight time of eight minutes, and once it returns to its base station, it takes around an hour to fully recharge (eight minutes on the dock will give it one minute in the air).

As Ring founder Jamie Siminoff explained during the preview event, the company has been trying to build a workable camera drone for around a decade, but couldn't overcome certain design challenges until the advancement of AI models that allow the device to handle most of the computing—from route programming to threat detection—via the cloud, so the drones can be smaller and lighter.

According to Ring, when setting up the Ring Drone Cam, you carry it around your house, allowing it to map the interior. It will "intelligently identify rooms and suggest patrol points: spots worth extra attention." When sent out on "patrol," the drone's AI pilot will travel between hotspots, sensing and avoiding furniture and other obstacles along the way.The Ring Drone Cam works with other Ring cameras, so if an alert is triggered somewhere in your home—say, a window opening unexpectedly—the drone will take off to investigate. It has a built-in security light that will make its presence known, so it can also act as a deterrent, though the screaming sound of its spinning propellers will accomplish that just as well.

According to Ring, the drone camera can deliver peace of mind whether you're home or away, and admittedly I do like the idea of being able to check on my pets or make sure no pipes have burst while I'm at work or on vacation (though admittedly you can get the same sort of monitoring without involving an AI device that looks like a mini version of the flying robots from The Terminator).

I admit that the Ring Drone Cam seems pretty cool, provided I don't think about it too much. I don't know that I really feel the need to have every inch of my home covered in security cameras, but I do like the idea that the drone could, for example, go to check out what's going on if one of my smoke alarms' temperature sensors reports that one spot in the house is all of a sudden hotter than it should be.

If you're ready to enter this brave new world of security, you'll have to wait a bit longer: The Ring Drone Camera isn't expected to ship until January 2027, but you can sign up to be alerted when it is available for preorder now.

Not everyone needs the company's most powerful models

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Anthropic has a new AI model, and it's more powerful than the Claude most people are using for chat. And that's precisely why the company doesn't actually recommend switching to it for everyday tasks.

Claude Fable 5.2, released Monday alongside the more restricted Mythos 5.2, is designed for some of the toughest work AI can handle, including advanced coding, scientific research and complex engineering projects.

The timing is significant. Anthropic is also preparing for a massive initial public offering, putting fresh attention on how the company plans to turn increasingly powerful AI into a profitable business.

For Claude users, though, the immediate question is simpler: what can Fable 5.2 actually do, and is it worth using instead of Opus?

Fable 5.2 is designed for projects that require more than generating an email, summarizing a document or answering a question.

Anthropic says its newest model can handle complicated technical work that would otherwise require extensive human effort. During prerelease testing, its models helped engineers complete difficult software migrations, design working electronic devices and tackle advanced physics problems.

One of the more interesting applications is using Fable as an AI advisor. Rather than asking Fable to handle every task, developers can have smaller Claude models consult it when they encounter a particularly difficult problem.

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

Fable can also act as an orchestrator, coordinating smaller models and assigning them simpler tasks while it handles the more complicated work.

For everyday users, the most practical applications could include analyzing complex research, working through difficult technical problems or managing projects that involve multiple steps and large amounts of information.

Here's where Anthropic's lineup gets confusing. Despite introducing Fable 5.2 as one of its most capable models, Anthropic recommends that most people continue using Claude Opus 5.5 for everyday coding and knowledge work.

The company describes Opus as its strongest daily driver, while Fable is intended for more ambitious technical challenges. That means someone using Claude for writing, research, brainstorming or routine coding probably doesn't need to switch.

Fable becomes more interesting when a task requires sustained reasoning, complicated problem-solving or coordination between multiple AI systems.

There are also cheaper models in the lineup. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 remain options for simpler work where speed and efficiency matter more than maximum capability.

The takeaway is that the most powerful Claude isn't automatically the best Claude for every job.

Anthropic has reduced the price of Fable compared with its previous version, but it remains more expensive than Opus.

Through the API, Fable 5.2 costs $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens. That's 20% less than Fable 5.1, although it's still twice the per-token price of Opus 5.5.

Anthropic also says the new model generates responses up to 30% faster than its predecessor. An optional fast mode offers even higher output speeds, but at twice the standard API token price.

For developers and businesses running large numbers of AI requests, those differences can add up quickly. If you run through your usage limits quickly, you might want to choose Opus 5.5 first.

For people using Claude through a subscription, access and usage limits also matter. Fable is available through supported Claude plans, although how much you can use depends on your subscription and any applicable usage credits.

Anthropic's latest model launch arrives at a particularly important moment for the company.

According to Reuters, Anthropic circulated IPO pricing information to banks before retracting it, saying the figures were inaccurate. The withdrawn proposal outlined a potential offering worth as much as $69.3 billion, although those numbers should not be treated as finalized.

The company is entering the public-market spotlight at a time when investors are scrutinizing the enormous cost of developing and operating advanced AI.

So, instead of offering one extremly powerful version of Claude for everyone, Anthropic is building a lineup designed for different types of work and different budgets.

Haiku and Sonnet can handle simpler, high-volume tasks. Opus serves as the everyday workhorse. Fable targets more demanding projects, while Mythos offers specialized capabilities to approved organizations working in fields such as cybersecurity and biomedical research.

It's a strategy that could help Anthropic serve more customers without requiring everyone to pay for its most expensive technology.

But it also creates a challenge: users need to understand why they should pay more for one model when another may already do everything they need.

As Anthropic moves toward its IPO, demonstrating that customers will pay for those additional capabilities could become just as important as achieving another impressive benchmark score.

If you're already using Claude Opus 5.5 for writing, research, brainstorming or everyday productivity, there's little reason to rush into Fable 5.2.

The new model is worth exploring if you're working on particularly difficult technical projects or tasks where existing AI models struggle to deliver reliable results.

For everyone else, Opus remains Anthropic's recommended starting point.

#3309. 10 Shows Like 'Minimum Wage' You Should Watch Next

Ross Johnson writes about television, film, and literature for Lifehacker. Ross has been an actor on stage, in commercials, and in independent films since childhood, and has written hundreds of articles and essays on genre literature and cinema for Barnes & Noble, Gizmodo, Kotaku, and Yahoo! Entertainment.Ross produces the Swan Songs film podcast and hosts The Sound of Tomorrow, a pop culture and current affairs radio show based in Rochester, New York, where he lives with his husband and dogs and supports the local arts and cinema scene. You can find him on Bluesky.

This is Streamalikes, where you can find a curated list of recommendations to stream based on what you already like.

Spinning off of a popular web series, Netflix's Minimum Wage is currently in the middle of a 28-episode first-season run. If that sounds like a lot of episodes for a show in 2026, keep in mind that they're generally less than 15 minutes each, which is perfect for your overloaded to-watch list—especially when they go down so easily. This cringe workplace mockumentary follows the crew of teenagers running a failing pizza place and making (you guessed it) minimum wage; they're under enormous pressure from their boss (Randall Park) to save the business and their one dumb source of income.

The punchy episodes will leave you plenty of time to explore other streaming shows dealing with the utter ridiculousness of the modern workplace. Here are 10 to get you started.

Workplace comedies usually revolve around white-collar office environments (The Mary Tyler Moore Show, 30 Rock, Parks and Recreation, etc.). Like Minimum Wage, Superstore instead follows the staff of Cloud 9, a generic big-box retailer. The show’s deep bench and diverse cast are largely focused on the jokes, but much of that comedy involves the relatable situation of working a job that demands commitment and a smiley attitude in the face of both entitled customers and obnoxious bosses. It's a different venue and age bracket, but a nutty workplace is a nutty workplace. Stream Superstore on Hulu and Peacock.

We're moving away from the workplace and aging things up a bit, but no worries: the name is a little ironic given that the codependent, co-habitating twenty-somethings of the title are hardly mature. Five friends are cohabiting in the childhood home of Samir (Malik Elassal), and dealing with the uniquely Gen-Z humiliations around dating, work, and even health insurance. Only one member of the group has an actual reasonably good job, while career paths for the others include being a temp, waiter, and a part-time ballet instructor. Stream Adults on Hulu.

This offbeat workplace comedy kicks off with a fabulous premise: Jeong Bok-dong (Kim Byung-chul) was a high-level director in a major corporation until one bad meeting saw him demoted. To president! ...of the company's failing Pegasus Mart offshoot. Bok-dong makes it his mission to get revenge by bankrupting the store, hiring eccentrics to execute eccentric, entirely whackadoo plans and accidentally getting Pegasus noticed by customers, who quickly make it more popular than ever. Think The Producers, but in retail. Stream Pegasus Market on Tubi.

It might sound a little (or a lot) niche, but we’ve seen enough headlines about the working conditions at many video game production houses to understand why a workplace comedy set against such a backdrop would make for a dark and juicy comedy. Charlotte Nicdao and Rob McElhenney are the leads, playing a brilliant workaholic and an unsociable egomaniac, respectively, and the chemistry between them gives the show more than enough spark. There's also a four-episode spin-off called Side Quest. Stream Mythic Quest.

A half-hour comedy-drama with an emphasis on the comedy, Gentefied follows three Mexican-American cousins who have built lives in Los Angeles, only to be faced with a new challenge: the looming gentrification of the neighborhood they helped to build via their family's taco shop. Gentefied has a baked-in sense of place and culture and a lot of heart; the second season is even better than the first. Stream Gentefied on Netflix.

Perhaps there's a bit of counter-programming in this dramedy about a couple of scrappy New York City outsiders, but there's a fundamental goofiness to this show about a couple of nice guys who are great at getting themselves into trouble, and equally good at talking themselves out of it. Bryan Greenberg plays Ben Epstein, a quiet guy with any number of big ideas, while Victor Rasuk plays the outgoing, often shameless Cam Calderon; together they manage a startup clothing business with the benefits of neither money nor experience, amiably hustling their way to success, maybe. Stream How to Make It in America on HBO Max and Netflix.

Debuting at the beginning of the Obama administration before getting a surprise revival just a couple of years ago, Party Down is an acclaimed cult sitcom for the ages—lots of laughs, low ratings, and always worth rediscovering. A group of six (or so) struggling LA actors and writers work as cater waiters for a fancy company, with every episode into a new and wildly absurd situation, even as their aspirations far outstrip their actual lives. Stream Party Down on Prime Video and Netflix.

A legitimate sitcom that just happens to be set in Northern Ireland during the violent Troubles of the 1990s, when clashes between nationalists and unionists frequently resulted in violence. It’s a fascinating contrast, brought to life by a writer and creator (Lisa McGee) who lived it. It’s also laugh-out-loud funny—though it doesn’t make any allowances for audiences unaccustomed to Irish accents, so don’t feel bad if you need subtitles until you get the hang of it. Erin, Orla, Clare, and Michelle are joined by James, the only male student at their Catholic girls' school, dealing with normal growing-up stuff in absurd times. This world is a far cry from that of Minimum Wage, but Lisa McGee's sense of the absurd connects both shows—if the setting is a bit more dramatic, the comedy is just as wonderfully silly. Stream Derry Girls on Netflix.

Not a comedy! But about as good an indication of where we are in the modern global workplace as you're likely to find. Hyuk‑jun is a young guy saddled with debt who signs on for some part-time work at a job agency...at 50x the going rate, no less (should've been a red flag). Each new assignment places him in new and increasingly horrific situations, with increasingly arbitrary-seeming rules. But, hey, in 2026, it's a living. Stream Dead-End Job on Netflix.

It's an office (obviously) and not a pizza joint, but the point here is kinda that white-collar jobs in the 21st century can be at least as soul-killing as working customer service. The Office inherited some of the finer tropes of the workplace comedy (mostly involving tossing together a group of weirdos overly invested in their jobs) while also launching a million mockumentary-style shows, running for nine seasons, and becoming one of the most popular shows of its era. Stream The Office on Peacock.

#3307. Rising Star Molly McCann On Finding Her Place In Panem For ‘The Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping’

Molly McCann has a lot to be excited about. The 15-year-old Irish actress has already built up a roster of credits including Bad Sisters and 2020 Sundance hit title Herself, but now she’s gearing up for her biggest project to date with The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, Lionsgate’s latest return to Suzanne Collins’ hugely popular dystopian universe.

McCann plays Louella McCoy, one of the female tributes from District 12 and a close ally of Haymitch, in a story set some 24 years before Katniss Everdeen’s story, the character famously played by Jennifer Lawrence more than a decade ago. Related Stories News 'Hunger Games: Sunrise On The Reaping' Getting Hot With $80M+ Opening Floor, Presales Ahead Of 'Wicked' - Box Office Update News Lionsgate & 3 Arts Set New Horror Banner Render Road Led By Luke Maxwell & Will Rowbotham - The Dish

“The hardest part for me was having to keep it a secret for a month,” McCann tells Deadline via Zoom from her family home in Dublin. “I just wanted to tell everyone.” Watch on Deadline

Sunrise on the Reaping, which bows worldwide on November 20, opens on the morning of the reaping of the 50th Hunger Games, when the Capitol demands twice the number of tributes – 48 children instead of 24. The story focuses on 16-year-old Haymitch, played by Joseph Zada, a clever and resourceful boy from District 12. (Woody Harrelson played an older Haymitch in the previous films.) Louella, who comes from the same district, and Haymitch are particularly close as they navigate their calling to the Hunger Games.

“Haymitch and Louella have such a special bond together and I think that Joe and I did a good job of recreating that and using the book to help us capture how close they were on screen,” she says.

The film boasts a stellar cast that also includes Mckenna Grace, Elle Fanning, Maya Hawke, Ralph Fiennes, Jesse Plemons and Glenn Close. Jennifer Lawrence and Josh Hutcherson, who played Peeta in the previous films, are also expected to return in a scene where an older Haymitch recounts his Hunger Game to them.

In the book’s epilogue, an older Haymitch notes that a young Katniss reminded him of Louella not only because of the two braids in her hair but also because of her “tough and smart” demeanor. “He calls them both sweetheart and says they look alike,” she says, adding that many of her friends kept asking her if she was playing a younger Katniss. “I was like, ‘not quite, no.’ They got so confused.”

And while McCann’s didn’t cross paths with Lawrence on set, she’s hopeful the star will enjoy her performance. “I think it’s really special that I get to share something like this with someone as incredible as Jennifer Lawrence,” she says.

McCann has been exposed to the acting world all her life. Her parents are both actors and her mother runs a stage school. This upbringing, she says, means she’s been comfortable on set from a very young age.

At the age of five, she was cast as one of the child actors in 2018 drama Rosie with Bad Sisters star Sarah Greene. A few years later McCann earned an Irish Film and Television (IFTA) nomination for Best Actress in a Supporting Role in Herself, which starred Claire Dunne and Harriet Walter. That Phyllida Lloyd-directed drama saw McCann play the daughter of a single mother (Dunne) who, after escaping an abusive partner, aims to rebuild her life in a unique manner.

Working with Lloyd, she says, was a formative experience. “She was such an amazing director and Harriet Walter is a legend. It was a great learning curve for me.”

McCann auditioned for Sunrise on the Reaping in early 2025, having only watched the original Hunger Games movies a few months earlier and she admits that she was unaware of how “massive” the fanbase is. “I think I would have been very nervous if I had known how big it is,” she says.

Sunrise on the Reaping brought a lot of firsts for McCann, including shooting in a studio – the film shot at Germany’s Studio Babelsberg – and dying her hair. “I didn’t realize that when you dye your hair, you see yourself so differently,” she says. “I just thought it was the coolest thing ever.”

Director Francis Lawrence became, she says, an important creative ally during the shoot and she praises his collaborative approach and willingness to discuss scenes with the young cast. “He was always open for discussion, which made it great to know I could talk through things with him,” she says. “It really gave a sense of security while doing the scenes.”

The biggest challenge for McKenna while filming were the reaping scenes. McCann says she studied the previous films to note expressions on the faces of Katniss (Lawrence) and Prim (Willow Shields) when they were called to participate in the Games.

“It was challenging to get the look down that was scared but also controlled because you didn’t want the Capitol to see you scared at any point because you didn’t want to look weak to them,” she says. “Francis would always tell me to use my eyes and put it all through my eyes and keep it really contained while I acted. I found that was one of the most challenging things because I wanted to get it so right and for it to come across exactly how it did in the old movies. I wanted to carry that on and keep it looking correct.”

Up next, McCann can be seen in The Butler, an action comedy with Tom Hollander and Jean Reno from director Tom Edmunds, which she shot before Hunger Games. The film sees Reno plays a former WWI commando turned butler whose peaceful life is upended by mobsters collecting an old debt. McCann plays Harriett, a girl being looked after by him. While she admits she can’t reveal much yet, she says “it’s quite Christmassy with lots of action-packed moments.”

As for next steps, McCann says she’d love to do a musical one day. “If someone ever did a musical movie version of Beetlejuice, I would just love to be Lydia. I love Beetlejuice. I think it’s fantastic.”

#3306. Andrew Ng: Unbiggen AI

The AI pioneer says it’s time for smart-sized, “data-centric” solutions to big issues

Andrew Ng was involved in the rise of massive deep learning models trained on vast amounts of data, but now he’s preaching small-data solutions.

Andrew Ng has serious street cred in artificial intelligence. He pioneered the use of graphics processing units (GPUs) to train deep learning models in the late 2000s with his students at Stanford University, cofounded Google Brain in 2011, and then served for three years as chief scientist for Baidu, where he helped build the Chinese tech giant’s AI group. So when he says he has identified the next big shift in artificial intelligence, people listen. And that’s what he told IEEE Spectrum in an exclusive Q&A.

Ng’s current efforts are focused on his company Landing AI, which built a platform called LandingLens to help manufacturers improve visual inspection with computer vision. He has also become something of an evangelist for what he calls the data-centric AI movement, which he says can yield “small data” solutions to big issues in AI, including model efficiency, accuracy, and bias.

The great advances in deep learning over the past decade or so have been powered by ever-bigger models crunching ever-bigger amounts of data. Some people argue that that’s an unsustainable trajectory. Do you agree that it can’t go on that way?

Andrew Ng: This is a big question. We’ve seen foundation models in NLP [natural language processing]. I’m excited about NLP models getting even bigger, and also about the potential of building foundation models in computer vision. I think there’s lots of signal to still be exploited in video: We have not been able to build foundation models yet for video because of compute bandwidth and the cost of processing video, as opposed to tokenized text. So I think that this engine of scaling up deep learning algorithms, which has been running for something like 15 years now, still has steam in it. Having said that, it only applies to certain problems, and there’s a set of other problems that need small data solutions.

When you say you want a foundation model for computer vision, what do you mean by that?

Ng: This is a term coined by Percy Liang and some of my friends at Stanford to refer to very large models, trained on very large data sets, that can be tuned for specific applications. For example, GPT-3 is an example of a foundation model [for NLP]. Foundation models offer a lot of promise as a new paradigm in developing machine learning applications, but also challenges in terms of making sure that they’re reasonably fair and free from bias, especially if many of us will be building on top of them.

What needs to happen for someone to build a foundation model for video?

Ng: I think there is a scalability problem. The compute power needed to process the large volume of images for video is significant, and I think that’s why foundation models have arisen first in NLP. Many researchers are working on this, and I think we’re seeing early signs of such models being developed in computer vision. But I’m confident that if a semiconductor maker gave us 10 times more processor power, we could easily find 10 times more video to build such models for vision.

Having said that, a lot of what’s happened over the past decade is that deep learning has happened in consumer-facing companies that have large user bases, sometimes billions of users, and therefore very large data sets. While that paradigm of machine learning has driven a lot of economic value in consumer software, I find that that recipe of scale doesn’t work for other industries.

It’s funny to hear you say that, because your early work was at a consumer-facing company with millions of users.

Ng: Over a decade ago, when I proposed starting the Google Brain project to use Google’s compute infrastructure to build very large neural networks, it was a controversial step. One very senior person pulled me aside and warned me that starting Google Brain would be bad for my career. I think he felt that the action couldn’t just be in scaling up, and that I should instead focus on architecture innovation.

“In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.” —Andrew Ng, CEO & Founder, Landing AI

I remember when my students and I published the first NeurIPS workshop paper advocating using CUDA, a platform for processing on GPUs, for deep learning—a different senior person in AI sat me down and said, “CUDA is really complicated to program. As a programming paradigm, this seems like too much work.” I did manage to convince him; the other person I did not convince.

Over the past year as I’ve been speaking to people about the data-centric AI movement, I’ve been getting flashbacks to when I was speaking to people about deep learning and scalability 10 or 15 years ago. In the past year, I’ve been getting the same mix of “there’s nothing new here” and “this seems like the wrong direction.”

How do you define data-centric AI, and why do you consider it a movement?

Ng: Data-centric AI is the discipline of systematically engineering the data needed to successfully build an AI system. For an AI system, you have to implement some algorithm, say a neural network, in code and then train it on your data set. The dominant paradigm over the last decade was to download the data set while you focus on improving the code. Thanks to that paradigm, over the last decade deep learning networks have improved significantly, to the point where for a lot of applications the code—the neural network architecture—is basically a solved problem. So for many practical applications, it’s now more productive to hold the neural network architecture fixed, and instead find ways to improve the data.

When I started speaking about this, there were many practitioners who, completely appropriately, raised their hands and said, “Yes, we’ve been doing this for 20 years.” This is the time to take the things that some individuals have been doing intuitively and make it a systematic engineering discipline.

The data-centric AI movement is much bigger than one company or group of researchers. My collaborators and I organized a data-centric AI workshop at NeurIPS, and I was really delighted at the number of authors and presenters that showed up.

You often talk about companies or institutions that have only a small amount of data to work with. How can data-centric AI help them?

Ng: You hear a lot about vision systems built with millions of images—I once built a face recognition system using 350 million images. Architectures built for hundreds of millions of images don’t work with only 50 images. But it turns out, if you have 50 really good examples, you can build something valuable, like a defect-inspection system. In many industries where giant data sets simply don’t exist, I think the focus has to shift from big data to good data. Having 50 thoughtfully engineered examples can be sufficient to explain to the neural network what you want it to learn.

When you talk about training a model with just 50 images, does that really mean you’re taking an existing model that was trained on a very large data set and fine-tuning it? Or do you mean a brand new model that’s designed to learn only from that small data set?

Ng: Let me describe what Landing AI does. When doing visual inspection for manufacturers, we often use our own flavor of RetinaNet. It is a pretrained model. Having said that, the pretraining is a small piece of the puzzle. What’s a bigger piece of the puzzle is providing tools that enable the manufacturer to pick the right set of images [to use for fine-tuning] and label them in a consistent way. There’s a very practical problem we’ve seen spanning vision, NLP, and speech, where even human annotators don’t agree on the appropriate label. For big data applications, the common response has been: If the data is noisy, let’s just get a lot of data and the algorithm will average over it. But if you can develop tools that flag where the data’s inconsistent and give you a very targeted way to improve the consistency of the data, that turns out to be a more efficient way to get a high-performing system.

“Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.” —Andrew Ng

For example, if you have 10,000 images where 30 images are of one class, and those 30 images are labeled inconsistently, one of the things we do is build tools to draw your attention to the subset of data that’s inconsistent. So you can very quickly relabel those images to be more consistent, and this leads to improvement in performance.

Could this focus on high-quality data help with bias in data sets? If you’re able to curate the data more before training?

Ng: Very much so. Many researchers have pointed out that biased data is one factor among many leading to biased systems. There have been many thoughtful efforts to engineer the data. At the NeurIPS workshop, Olga Russakovsky gave a really nice talk on this. At the main NeurIPS conference, I also really enjoyed Mary Gray’s presentation, which touched on how data-centric AI is one piece of the solution, but not the entire solution. New tools like Datasheets for Datasets also seem like an important piece of the puzzle.

One of the powerful tools that data-centric AI gives us is the ability to engineer a subset of the data. Imagine training a machine-learning system and finding that its performance is okay for most of the data set, but its performance is biased for just a subset of the data. If you try to change the whole neural network architecture to improve the performance on just that subset, it’s quite difficult. But if you can engineer a subset of the data you can address the problem in a much more targeted way.

When you talk about engineering the data, what do you mean exactly?

Ng: In AI, data cleaning is important, but the way the data has been cleaned has often been in very manual ways. In computer vision, someone may visualize images through a Jupyter notebook and maybe spot the problem, and maybe fix it. But I’m excited about tools that allow you to have a very large data set, tools that draw your attention quickly and efficiently to the subset of data where, say, the labels are noisy. Or to quickly bring your attention to the one class among 100 classes where it would benefit you to collect more data. Collecting more data often helps, but if you try to collect more data for everything, that can be a very expensive activity.

For example, I once figured out that a speech-recognition system was performing poorly when there was car noise in the background. Knowing that allowed me to collect more data with car noise in the background, rather than trying to collect more data for everything, which would have been expensive and slow.

What about using synthetic data, is that often a good solution?

Ng: I think synthetic data is an important tool in the tool chest of data-centric AI. At the NeurIPS workshop, Anima Anandkumar gave a great talk that touched on synthetic data. I think there are important uses of synthetic data that go beyond just being a preprocessing step for increasing the data set for a learning algorithm. I’d love to see more tools to let developers use synthetic data generation as part of the closed loop of iterative machine learning development.

Do you mean that synthetic data would allow you to try the model on more data sets?

Ng: Not really. Here’s an example. Let’s say you’re trying to detect defects in a smartphone casing. There are many different types of defects on smartphones. It could be a scratch, a dent, pit marks, discoloration of the material, other types of blemishes. If you train the model and then find through error analysis that it’s doing well overall but it’s performing poorly on pit marks, then synthetic data generation allows you to address the problem in a more targeted way. You could generate more data just for the pit-mark category.

“In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models.” —Andrew Ng

Synthetic data generation is a very powerful tool, but there are many simpler tools that I will often try first. Such as data augmentation, improving labeling consistency, or just asking a factory to collect more data.

To make these issues more concrete, can you walk me through an example? When a company approaches Landing AI and says it has a problem with visual inspection, how do you onboard them and work toward deployment?

Ng: When a customer approaches us we usually have a conversation about their inspection problem and look at a few images to verify that the problem is feasible with computer vision. Assuming it is, we ask them to upload the data to the LandingLens platform. We often advise them on the methodology of data-centric AI and help them label the data.

One of the foci of Landing AI is to empower manufacturing companies to do the machine learning work themselves. A lot of our work is making sure the software is fast and easy to use. Through the iterative process of machine learning development, we advise customers on things like how to train models on the platform, when and how to improve the labeling of data so the performance of the model improves. Our training and software supports them all the way through deploying the trained model to an edge device in the factory.

How do you deal with changing needs? If products change or lighting conditions change in the factory, can the model keep up?

Ng: It varies by manufacturer. There is data drift in many contexts. But there are some manufacturers that have been running the same manufacturing line for 20 years now with few changes, so they don’t expect changes in the next five years. Those stable environments make things easier. For other manufacturers, we provide tools to flag when there’s a significant data-drift issue. I find it really important to empower manufacturing customers to correct data, retrain, and update the model. Because if something changes and it’s 3 a.m. in the United States, I want them to be able to adapt their learning algorithm right away to maintain operations.

In the consumer software Internet, we could train a handful of machine-learning models to serve a billion users. In manufacturing, you might have 10,000 manufacturers building 10,000 custom AI models. The challenge is, how do you do that without Landing AI having to hire 10,000 machine learning specialists?

So you’re saying that to make it scale, you have to empower customers to do a lot of the training and other work.

Ng: Yes, exactly! This is an industry-wide problem in AI, not just in manufacturing. Look at health care. Every hospital has its own slightly different format for electronic health records. How can every hospital train its own custom AI model? Expecting every hospital’s IT personnel to invent new neural-network architectures is unrealistic. The only way out of this dilemma is to build tools that empower the customers to build their own models by giving them tools to engineer the data and express their domain knowledge. That’s what Landing AI is executing in computer vision, and the field of AI needs other teams to execute this in other domains.

Is there anything else you think it’s important for people to understand about the work you’re doing or the data-centric AI movement?

Ng: In the last decade, the biggest shift in AI was a shift to deep learning. I think it’s quite possible that in this decade the biggest shift will be to data-centric AI. With the maturity of today’s neural network architectures, I think for a lot of the practical applications the bottleneck will be whether we can efficiently get the data we need to develop systems that work well. The data-centric AI movement has tremendous energy and momentum across the whole community. I hope more researchers and developers will jump in and work on it.

This article appears in the April 2022 print issue as “Andrew Ng, AI Minimalist.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

#3304. There’s a Good Reason the NYC Marathon Winners Wore These Watches

Over 60,000 runners crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon last week. When you think of the elites fighting for a spot on the podium, you might expect to see only the priciest, most feature-packed GPS watches money can buy—historically, this meant the most premium Garmin Forerunners. Looking at the wrists of this year's New York City Marathon podium finishers, though,  you’ll see that Garmin—the name most recreational runners reach for by default—was far from the only brand on the course.

Here are the watches I’ve been able to confirm among the top NYC Marathon finishers:

Men's winner, Andreas Almgren: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Men's runner-up, Yemaneberhan Crippa: Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro (sponsored)

Women's runner-up, Jessica McClain: Garmin Forerunner 570 (sponsored)

Women's third place, Hellen Obiri: Coros Pace 4 (sponsored)

Nonbinary winner, Ryan Montgomery: Suunto Race 3S (almost certainly sponsored, since this watch was released last month)

An important disclaimer: I haven't spoken with any of these athletes. What follows is my opinion, based on what I know running watches offer the people who wear them.

"Garmin" has long been the default answer to "what running watch should I buy?" It earned that spot with reliable GPS, excellent software, and a huge ecosystem. And on this podium, it's represented by a Forerunner 570—a great watch, but at a price tag most runners would struggle to justify.

Of course, sponsorships muddy the water, since athletes wear what their sponsors put on their wrists. But that's exactly the point: Other brands are investing in elite runners because they believe their products can stand next to Garmin's, and it looks like they’re making the right bet.

It's fair to ask whether Garmin's grip is loosening. The company has increasingly pushed toward the fanciest watches with the most features at higher and higher price points. The Forerunner 570 starts north of $500. Meanwhile, COROS, Amazfit, and others are proving that a perfectly solid, competitive watch doesn't need to cost that much. Is Garmin still the best running watch overall? For ecosystem, polish, and depth of features, it's still a strong contender. But "best" no longer means "the only serious option," and the gap between Garmin and the field is narrower than it has been in years. Sponsored or not, seeing two Coros Pace 4s and an Amazfit Cheetah 2 Pro among the top finishers is worth noting.

You don’t need an expensive watch to be elite—just look at the cheap running watches worn by the men who broke the sub-two-hour barrier at the London Marathon this past spring. Training load scores, recovery metrics, maps, music, and smart notifications are nice, but they're extras. If you're shopping for a watch, spend your money on the basics being done right, and don't feel pressured to pay for features you'll never use. Everything besides your time and pace is icing on the cake.

Whichever brand you choose, focus on these basics in your running watch:

The New York City Marathon podium shows a running-watch market that's a bit more competitive and intriguing than the era of "just buy a Garmin" suggests. Garmin is still excellent, but now we’re seeing proof that Coros, Amazfit, and Suunto are all making watches good enough for the fastest humans on the planet. If they can trust those watches on their biggest days, the rest of us can probably trust them with our Saturday long runs.

Smart city deployments have historically relied on cameras, sensors, and dashboards that capture data without delivering timely insight. Edge AI changes this by letting inference happen close to where data is generated. This supports faster decisions, stronger data sovereignty, and lower operating costs than cloud-only designs. This guide traces the progression from automation and perception to prediction, agentic coordination, and physical AI, where urban systems continuously perceive conditions, reason about them, and act within a tiered edge architecture spanning far-edge sensors, regional infrastructure, and the cloud. It also outlines the durability, security, and interoperability requirements that production-grade edge hardware and software must meet to support public safety, mobility, and infrastructure use cases at city scale.

#3301. ‘The Empress’ Creator Katharina Eyssen On Feeling A “Mix Of Emotions” As Netflix Hit Ends, Spin-Off Potential & Upcoming Series ‘Witches’

EXCLUSIVE: Katharina Eyssen is reflecting on the “mix of emotions” around the end of Netflix‘s royal hit The Empress, but she’s already got one eye on what the future holds.

The German showrunner told Deadline she has considered how expand the European period drama franchise, though nothing is currently in the works as she moves on to her next Netflix series, Witches. We revealed news of the show, which will be one of the streamer’s biggest budget European originals and is about German witch hunts in the 1700s, back in February.

As for the future The Empress (Die Kaiserin), which stars Devrim Lingnau as Empress Elisabeth of Austria in 19th century Europe, Eyssen has looked at another Netflix showrunner for inspiration. “I’m impressed by what Shonda Rhimes is doing with Bridgerton, with one spin-off here and another there,” she said in an exclusive interview with Deadline. Watch on Deadline Related Stories News Netflix's 'The Perfect Neighbor' Beats 'Mr Nobody Against Putin' To Top Prize At UK Grierson Documentary Awards News Netflix Refuses To Remove Russell Brand Stand-Up Special Featuring Crude Sex Joke

“Some of the [Empress] characters are finished, given where we leave them historically, but there could be possibilities to go back in time and tell an origin story, or a childhood or youth story. There is also material in the stories of Elizabeth’s children. I’m not pitching this, but there would be material for anyone who is interested. Perhaps we can all sleep on it and see how Season 3 does.”

The third and final season of The Empress launches globally tomorrow (November 12) with a world premiere held in Berlin last night. Eyssen and her husband, Robert Eyssen, who is the series’ co-showrunner, were among those attending at the Delphi Filmpalast alongside the likes of Lingnau and co-star Philip Froissant. Here are some images from the event.

Per a trailer released last month, Season 3 sees Elisabeth (or Sisi) dealing with the rejection and unfaithful behavior of Emperor Franz (Philip Froissant), who returns traumatized from the Sardinian War. Sisi decides to leave Vienna and set off to a distant island to recover her health and distance herself from her European troubles, and soon meets the leader of the Hungarian revolution, Count Andrássy (Dejan Bućin). They immediately share a strong physical and emotional attraction.

Eyssen reflected on the show’s ending, saying it makes “total sense” to stop at this stage. “It’s a mix of emotions,” she added. “I’m relieved and happy that we are able to finish the series on our own terms. We knew while I was writing it that the story really has an ending. On the other hand, I’m sad. The working relationship with so many people in this particular ensemble and this particular combination has come to an end.

“It’s satisfying to end on a high note, while the show is still successful, people are still enjoying it, we are still friends and we still love the work. The idea of a band breaking up while it is still on top always sounded strange to me, but now it makes total sense. It would feel awful to be cancelled or to drag the show on for another season when nobody was enjoying it any more.”

Eyssen, who was showrunner and head writer through the three seasons, praised series star Lingnau, saying their working life together had been a “gift,” and added execs at Netflix had told her “the character is incredibly popular” with audiences.

She also extolled the virtues of her husband, who edited Season 1 before becoming a more hands-on exec producer in Season 2, taking over the entire visual side of the production. “Writing the show and then creatively leading every part of it is too much for one person,” said Eyssen of her Season 1 experience.

Staying respectful during creative process

Given the size of The Empress and the relative scarcity of German Netflix original, The Empress was always going to be heavily scrutinized by both the streamer and creative teams. Eyssen, who is one of a relatively small number of European showrunners who’ve worked at this scale, gave a measured assessment of how the process worked.

She began by referencing her time making 2018 Netflix miniseries Holiday Secrets, aka Zeit der Geheimnisse, before noting that the scale of The Empress meant there was “inevitably conflict, which is completely normal.”

This was partly down her and the producer, Sommerhaus Serien, having never attempted a historical drama of such ambition, and the effects of the Covid-19 lockdown, which “created disagreements” over “how European” the show should be, whether it should be “edgier” and how brazenly commercial it would be on screen.

“I was lucky to work with Eva van Leeuwen, who is now the head of German series at Netflix,” she added. “During Season 1, she was the executive on our show. We deeply respect each other. Through all the ups and downs and the disagreements, which are normal in any creative process, we always remained good colleagues, friends even.

“I respect Netflix for trusting me and my team. The show is as good as it is because sometimes they followed us, other times I came around to their point of view. We had to find common ground, and that made the show what it is.”

Van Leeuwen is also attached to Witches, along with exec producer Scarlett Lacey, who wrote the original script and treatment for Paramount’s 2001 movie the Save the Last Dance, is another returning. The Empress producer Sommerhaus is making the series.

“I have always wanted to do this,” said Eyssen. “After our first project with Netflix – a small miniseries, really a three-part film – they asked in 2019 whether we wanted to work together again, perhaps on a historical series. I said I wanted to tell the story of the witch hunts in Germany, a dark and significant chapter of our history that is not as well known because we have other very dark chapters in our history. I asked, ‘What about the witch craze?'”

Quizzed on when Witches might debut, Eyssen said: “I’m writing at the moment, which is always the hardest part. Sometimes I think, ‘Never,’ because writing is so difficult, but hopefully we can get it done within the next two years.”

Speaking of timeframes, the interview also stretched into the debate over the long lengths of time between seasons on streaming services – The Empress‘s third season launch tomorrow comes two years after the second, for example.

The likes of Katherine Pope, the Sony Pictures Television President, have in recent years advocated for shorter gaps, while the fall-off in ratings between first and second seasons on Netflix shows such as Beef, The Four Seasons and A Good Girl’s Guide To Murder have added fuel to fire around the “sophomore slump” phenomena.

On a personal level, Eyssen said the gap “should be shorter,” but put this down to a German TV-making sensibility of productions taking as long as needed. “Now I understand more, partly because of my own behaviour as a viewer: Two years is a long time. You need a very strong commitment from fans and viewers for them to return to a show after two years. I respect and understand that.

“Showrunners working on recurring shows of this size was a new concept for us in Germany, so we did not yet have the tools to work more efficiently. Now we may be experienced enough to get it done more quickly. We can distribute the work differently. Perhaps I would not need to be on set as much, and I could start writing earlier. We are learning as we go.”

The Empress may be leaving the court, but Eyssen sounds ready for her next her royal appointment.

If you've tried breathable bed sheets, oscillating fans and frozen pillows but you still wake up sweaty, I've found the solution. The Orion Sleep System, now with $600 off in Orion's Black Friday sale, is a smart cooling system that helps defeat night sweats by actively adjusting the temperature as you sleep.

One of the best smart beds you can buy online, this clever mattress cover is fitted with a series of (imperceptible) water tubes that cool or heat throughout the night. That means a sudden flush of cold if night sweats are coming on, or a gentle warming if things get too chilly.

This is just a cover, so you might need to buy a new bed to go with it — I recommend our best mattress guide for our top rated suggestions. But with $600 off in the Black Friday mattress sales, there has never been a better time to shop the Orion.

When we review any mattress, temperature regulation is a key concern. It refers to how well a mattress can kick out excess heat so you don't wake up at 3 a.m. feeling uncomfortably sweaty.

Most of the best mattresses in a box achieve this through cooling materials. That is, copper-infused foams or phase change material (PCM).

The Orion takes a different approach. This smart mattress cover is fitted with a series of water tubes, which connect back to a control hub. During the night, the water flowing through those pipes either cools down or warms up, so you stay at just the right temperature.

And this sci-fi-esque sleep system is impressively effective. I purposely warmed myself up to see if the cooling kicked in (the only time you'll ever catch me doing nighttime jumping jacks) and was greeted by a flush of coolness. For hot flashes and night sweats, this is a dream.

Most of the time, however, the Orion delivers the kind of comfort you hardly notice. It's climbing into a bed that feels just right, sleeping through the night, and waking up feeling snug all the way down to your toes.

While the temperature regulation impressed me, I was less enthused by the Orion's sleep tracking. At $250 extra for a year's subscription, I think you can get better results for less with the Fitbit Air or Withings Sleep Analyzer. Or, for cooling and tracking, there's another solution...

I'm currently testing the Eight Sleep Pod 6, which uses water to cool and heat your mattress to just the right temperature. It's more expensive than the Orion — although you can save up to $200 in the pre-Black Friday sale and get a queen for $2,699 (was $2,899) — but the integrated sleep tracking is accurate and intuitive, delivering detailed insight into your rest. A subscription is required and starts from $17/month.
