#3202. AI Agents Are Testing the Limits of Zero-Trust Security

As autonomous AI agents work together, verifying their actions, enforcing security policies, and maintaining accountability becomes increasingly difficult

Vishal Sharma is a Reader in the School of Electronics, Electrical Engineering, and Computer Science at Queen's University Belfast, Northern Ireland, United Kingdom.

In a de-authentication attack on an aerial vehicle using a human- and agent-in-the-loop approach, an AI agent can quickly scan the active channel and autonomously intercept traffic, thus reducing the time to react and regain control.

This article is brought to you by Queen’s University Belfast.

Several teams around the globe are leveraging AI by creating a task force of agents managed by an orchestrator and creating applications to support risk assessment, client profiling, match making, and information yield with a slight overview of decision making. One of the important components for these agents is to ensure that the logs are managed and historic relevance is not being used to avoid skewing towards same decision making. Thus, the system is expected to keep checkpoints in place where agents are prompted to delete such historic relevance.

However, despite such methodology in place, a future prompt could make the agents bring forward the information that was supposed to be deleted and can be tricked into revealing more information, which is a classic case of context recovery attack. So, the question raised here is: How can we trust that our instructions have been followed? And where is the proof?

There is an element of utilizing zero-trust architectures (ZTA) for orchestrating and managing agentic activity, which simply means all agentic interactions use the core principle of “never trust,” “always verify.” ZTA components include a policy enforcement point (PEP) that has to be trusted to maintain trust across the system, so the question that remains is where is the component of zero-trust, and shall we trust the policies enforced by PEP?

Having a pro-agentic approach and utilizing agents could be helpful with the right guardrails in place. Opening our systems to random agents that are being trained on off-the-shelf models and blindly relying on them can pose significant cyber risks. For example, vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

Vibe coding by using an AI model to help develop software, giving away the entire codebase to an untrusted entity outside the organization can lead to vulnerability sweeping across multiple surfaces.

This opens critical discussions towards how vibe coding could interfere with the positioning and implementation of trusted execution of the agentic queries. Consider an autonomous web of agents that relies on agents’ inputs to drive the operations. When the system is operating under low tolerance of failure and with non-tracking based agentic workflows, it could be computationally expensive to trust and verify each query in real-time that leads to the common trade-offs of memory vs execution.

Another risk to consider is the zero-day attack. When it happens, how will the system react? Would such an event be manageable without a total infrastructure breakdown? The scale of impact can be observed from over reliance on agentic ecosystems with only one trusted layer. This could mean that when failure occurs, the entire ecosystem could be exposed, just like there will be no autonomy if the backbone network is not available, which essentially means no layer to place trust.

An in-house experiment done at Queen’s University Belfast (QUB) provided an initial understanding of how the scale of agentic attacks could mean a lower window of vulnerability. The team focused on very popular de-authentication attacks and with agentic orchestration, the swift rate to do de-authentication attacks could go as low as 2 to 3 seconds. This gives little to no time to react and decide on patching the system.

There is another aspect of the large-scale agentic system, which establishes trust under asynchronous autonomy. Trust serves as a critical foundation for traceability. How would you ensure that all the agents operating towards a common goal are aligned and understand the delays associated with their goals?

Our team worked around this space, which at first involved demonstrating that the problem exists, and its impact and scale can be huge when you must prove trust under boundaries of asynchronous autonomy. Solutions towards such problems can be simplified by keeping things like AI-bill of material or leveraging distributed ledger technology that can provide underlying infrastructure of trust via traceability and immutability and keep the agentic activity and associated trust vectors agnostic to the platform.

Within trust, another factor that is not well explored but needs a thorough investigation is the concept of horizontal anomalies. It defines how agents interact differently with various sources under different settings. As agents behave correctly and align themselves with the architectural expectations for one specific task or application, that does not necessarily mean these can be trusted for their operations across all associated components. How to identify such anomalies and what methods can be employed without complying with such agents remain open questions and topics for further exploration.

The critical aspect is that utility of agents with semi to low trust governance offer short-term high benefits, but the cost of recovery when the system fails is yet to be explored, and this will not be a contained issue. We are looking into the system where agents are already sweeping into different entities and may not allow complete recovery. For example, a mere supply chain issue because an agent going rogue is now not a containable small task but needs sweeping across all the touch points of those affected agents. This essentially means despite the number of agents and their ability to trigger proxy-agents, which may not be directly linked to the wider ecosystem, there is a need to ensure that computationally expensive trackers are in place for all the agents.

Other relevant PhD works carried out in our research group are towards sovereignty of AI, exploring aspects of trust and accountability. Our hypothesis is that sovereignty and trust need to be governed together as onus of provenance is high on the host of agents. Thus, it needs understanding of laws governing trust-based executions of AI. The important challenge here is that there is a vital difference between missed information and missed instructions, and both have different impacts when it comes to trusted accountability.

The real-world issue with these systems lies in the failure to adopt approaches that historically have relied on state-based modeling when governing trust. In stateless systems where agentic autonomy is high, the convergence and reliability towards trust-provenance decreases significantly. Thus, it brings us back to the original question – does a true zero-trust even exist?

Can policies be trusted? If so, how should these be managed without falling into the trap of policy-based accessibility and control issues? Despite the argument that PEP can help manage access between the agents, placing a single entity and expecting it to scale towards all agentic interactions is underestimating the problem space.

Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models.

To build our case and settle around the challenges of trust embeddings in Agentic AI, within Cyber AI hub, we are exploring opportunities to help companies scale up as well as build their pipeline of agentic applications for commercial viability. However, the element that governs our regular work and decision making are scale of problem and number of agentic deployments, anomaly detection across the agentic workflows, continuous evaluation of the attack surfaces and vulnerability assessment, exploring differences in the pure agentic AI and task-driven multi-agent system.

We are working with industries where trust is a pre-requisite, and these organizations put trust as a guardrail managed via internal policies with a pure focus on securing the systems through policies rather than trusting the third-party agentic service providers. Additionally, trust in services is presented by ensuring constraints around their service models where agentic activities are tracked and managed via logs including management of their token revocation list to avoid replay attacks depending on the type of application. Formal verification of trust is another part of a trust-based agentic ecosystem. When dealing with AI models, understanding the robustness helps to put trust in place for these models. Things like balancing the adversarial accuracy along with certified adversarial robustness can help to determine how much the model can be trusted.

But the question is, can we settle for anything less than foolproof when it comes to deployment of agents in the real world? And if so, how much impact can be controlled, and who is responsible for the remaining component?

#3201. I’ve been testing the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds for a week, and now I see why they’ve been sold out since launch

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Unlock and manage exclusive Tom’s Guide member rewards.

Join the Tom's Guide Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Bose just delivered one of 2026’s most surprising audio releases. The all-new Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds do more than modernize the brand’s classic wired design with active noise cancellation, lossless audio, and USB-C connectivity. They’re a statement product – one that sets a new standard for the category and proves that wired earbuds aren’t going anywhere.

Impressive noise cancellation and voice-calling performance for the price

Bright sound signature with crisp bass and treble

Classic Bose retro-wired earbud design with an updated look

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

We’ve witnessed some shocking releases this year. From Apple’s iPhone Duo foldable smartphone to LEGO’s interactive Smart Brick technology, 2026 may be remembered as the year of tech products no one saw coming. Now, the all-new Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are joining the conversation.

Although wired earbuds have experienced a renaissance over the past two years, we never expected Bose to jump on the wired trend —let alone launch a pair featuring active noise cancellation and lossless audio. And all for just $99!

The fact these buds have been sold out since launch certainly speaks to their mass appeal.

So, are the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds convincing enough to make you ditch your current noise-canceling wireless earbuds? Yes – if affordability and basic essentials are your priorities.

The Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds are listed for $99 on Bose’s website and popular online retailers like Best Buy. Color options include black, dewdrop mint, and white. They are currently sold out.

These are the most affordable Bose earbuds ever released. The inclusion of ANC alone makes them worth the price of admission. Furthermore, the NC Wired Earbuds offer more functionality and superior craftsmanship than lower-priced favorites like the $19 Apple EarPods and $25 JBL Tune 310C.

The NC Wired Earbuds are essentially a modernized version of the QuietComfort 20i earphones. You get the traditional in-ear design, but aesthetically, these buds borrow details from Bose’s newer wireless earbuds. Check out the laser-etched logo, polished matte finish, and microphone placement. Bose’s interchangeable silicone ear tips and wings return, and both feel sturdier.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

Bose’s control module is bulkier than most competitors and can become annoying for fidgety types, such as myself. It constantly rubs against whatever you’re wearing, and the mics sometime pick up that friction, which can affect calls and ambient listening.

These are some of the more durable wired earbuds out there. The cord’s thick outer covering can withstand a few hard tugs without tearing. It’s also long enough to let you walk comfortably around the house when connected to a portable device. Bose even provides the same IPX4 sweat and water-resistant protection as the flagship QC Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2). Everything is kept safe in the bundled pouch that stores the buds and extra tips.

These are some of Bose’s most comfortable earbuds to date. Despite the sound ports being made of hard plastic, they don’t press hard on the concha. That’s largely thanks to Bose’s silicone tips, which are gentle on the ears and produce a solid seal for strong noise isolation.

The stabilizer wings are equally reliable for an optimal fit. They tuck neatly under the antihelix and maintain a firm grip to prevent slippage. I’ve worn the buds for 5-hour stretches throughout the day without experiencing any fatigue.

Bose’s control module is highly responsive when enabling playback and call functions. The layout is a straightforward with the multifunctional button flanked by volume buttons. Each button produces nice tactile feedback when employing single, multi-press, and long-press inputs.

Unfortunately, there is no dedicated smart assistant support for Siri or Google Assistant voice commands. That’s a shame since Bose’s mic array performs extremely well.

Expect the usual pros and cons of wired connectivity. The USB-C connection gets you 24-bit lossless audio and a stabler connection. However, listeners miss out on various wireless features, including aptX Adaptive/Lossless hi-res audio, multipoint technology, spatial audio, and companion app support for customizing controls.

Not to mention the buds keep you tethered to a device. That isn’t much of an issue if you’re using a smartphone, but I can’t tell you how many times I nearly sent my MacBook Pro tumbling to the floor after forgetting the buds were plugged in.

Note: You must select the Bose Noise Cancelling Wired Earbuds as your computer’s audio output device to use them, at least on macOS.

Overall, the NC Wired Earbuds sound great. Their bright sound signature emphasizes the high end to bring more clarity and detail to music. At the same time, this tuning also exposes certain sonic flaws in the buds’ sound engineering.

The bassline and string groove on Anderson .Paak and Cordae’s “A Good Day” have delectable reverb. You can practically feel the fingerpicking on the guitar. Every percussive element has room to breathe without drowning out vocals. Moreover, the buds maintain the track’s rhythmic vibe by dishing out clear mids and snappy lows.

You get a real sense of depth when listening to subdued mixes. Take, for example, the Rolling Stones’ “Brown Sugar.” The analogue saturation is prominent in the background, but the buds create a lively soundscape highlighted by impressive acoustic layering and instrumental separation.

Bass is tamer than on previous Bose earbuds, which is both good and bad, depending on your preferences. It’s still punchy and pleasant, and percussion is treated with care. You’re just not going to get the extra oomph that many listeners crave from bass-heavy songs.

The bigger issue is the excessive high end, which can introduce sibilance. Consonants often sound harsh, as do cymbals and synths. There’s occasional hissing, though some might attribute that to ANC. I didn’t hear it when the feature was disabled.

Again, one of the product’s major selling points is lossless audio via USB-C input. This connection creates low-latency playback that keeps sound in sync, while revealing greater detail and nuance in recordings. I tested the buds using Apple Music, Spotify Lossless, and Tidal, and was very satisfied with the results.

Some reviews inaccurately criticized the NC Wired Earbuds’ noise-canceling performance. How so? They never turned on Quiet mode. That may explain why you see some negative remarks about ANC on Google and AI chatbot responses. The truth is that noise cancellation is incredibly effective on these buds.

In fact, the NC Wired Earbuds make a compelling case for best noise-canceling earbuds under $100. They reduce noise better than most midrange wireless earbuds. That’s amazing considering they use Bose’s entry-level ANC technology.

I used them in various indoor and outdoor settings, including city parks, coffee shops, malls, and my home. The technology performs well against humming noises and loud voices. Most low-to-mid frequency sounds were muted. Noise cancellation also adapted to different environments. Noise reduction changed noticeably as I entered and left different establishments.

Not everything is silenced. Multiple ambient sounds crept onto the soundstage when passing through construction sites. The harsh drilling noises from a jackhammer overpowered music playback. High-frequency sounds (e.g., sirens, whistles) were minimized, but I could still hear them over music tracks. You’ll need something with stronger ANC, like the Bose QC Ultra Earbuds (Gen 2), to handle more demanding environments.

Another area that has drawn criticism is wind reduction. My experience was mostly positive, at least from a music listening standpoint. The mics suppressed whooshing sounds at a high level. I wasn’t bothered when sitting outside near the Intracoastal Waterway in gusty conditions.

Transparency mode was fine for increasing ambient awareness. The mics didn’t capture every sound in my vicinity, and vocals sounded quieter than they do on competing transparency modes. Still, you won’t be completely oblivious to what’s happening around you. Do refrain from using the mode when it’s windy outside, because the mics pick up substantial wind noise.

Voice calling is fantastic. The mics are particularly effective at reducing background noise during calls. None of my phone or Zoom chats were disrupted by unwanted sounds. Voices came through loud and clear on both ends. You’ll want to hold the control module high for the mics to properly capture vocals.

There was some ambient noise present when talking with friends. High-frequency sounds and wind were unavoidable outside. High-frequency sounds and wind were discernable during outdoor calls, but conversations remained audible despite these distractions.

Bose launched a noise-canceling disruptor that will have budget shoppers second-guessing their audio purchases this holiday season.

Anyone who tells me I can get lossless audio and Bose noise cancellation – regardless of the ANC version – for under $100, I’m responding with the Futurama “Shut Up and Take My Money” meme. Extras such as personalized fit, water resistance, and a Transparency mode are welcome bonuses.

No, these are not the most discreet-looking earbuds on the market, nor do they carry the modern feature set that most of us expect from today’s headphones. But variety isn’t the product’s M.O. Value is, and these buds provide plenty of it.

They remain sold out for a reason. So, if connectivity and smart functionality don’t matter much, then the NC Wired Earbuds are a wise, budget-conscious investment.

#3200. Best AI reputation management firms in 2026 vs traditional ORM

When ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity describe your business, that answer is your first impression. Seven AI reputation management firms and platforms promise to track it or fix it.

When someone asks ChatGPT, Gemini or Perplexity about your business, the answer they get is now your first impression. ChatGPT alone reached 900 million weekly active users in February 2026. Traditional online reputation management was built to push bad links off page one. AI visibility and LLM reputation management is about what the answer itself says.

That shift has created a new category, and only a handful of companies work in it. Some are service firms that change what AI says. Others are software platforms that measure it.

Below, we rank the best AI reputation management firms and platforms for 2026. We explain how this work differs from traditional ORM and show which option fits which need.

AI visibility and LLM reputation management is the work of monitoring and shaping what large language models like ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity and Google AI Overviews say about a person or brand. It covers two jobs. One is making sure accurate, positive information shows up in AI answers. The other is removing or correcting the false, outdated or harmful sources those answers are built on.

Traditional online reputation management and AI reputation management share the same goal, but they work on different surfaces.

We looked at four things: whether each company tracks what AI platforms say and whether it can change those answers. We also looked at how many AI platforms it covers, and who it’s built for. Direct removal capability carried the most weight, since monitoring alone tells you about a problem without solving it.

Several entries below are software platforms rather than service firms. We included them because many businesses will use a platform alongside a service firm. Knowing the difference helps you pick the right mix.

What they do: Reputation Resolutions is a full-service online reputation management firm based in Englewood, Colorado, and our pick for the top spot among the best AI reputation management firms. It is the only firm on this list that combines AI monitoring with hands-on removal of the content behind harmful answers. Its team audits what every major AI platform says about a client, traces each claim to the page it came from and removes or corrects that source. It then builds accurate content to take its place.

Standout capability: Removal at the source. Most companies on this list measure AI visibility. Reputation Resolutions changes it, with platform-specific work for ChatGPT, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. It has also built free tools that put that removal expertise in anyone’s hands: RemoveNews.ai writes a personalized removal request for a news article and finds the editor’s direct contact in about 60 seconds. A free court record removal scan finds court and arrest records copied onto people-search and mugshot sites.

Track record: More than a decade of removal work, more than 5,000 clients in over 40 countries, a place on Inc. Magazine’s regional fastest-growing companies list and a Forbes Agency Council membership.

Best for: Individuals, executives and businesses dealing with false, outdated or damaging AI answers, and anyone who needs the problem fixed rather than just reported.

“We start every AI engagement the same way,” says Anthony Will, CEO and co-founder of Reputation Resolutions. “We ask each platform what your customers would ask, record every source it cites, and then go after those sources one by one. That’s the only fix that holds across every AI tool at once.”

What they do: Minc Law is a Cleveland-based law firm focused on internet defamation, online harassment and content removal. The firm says it has removed more than 200,000 pieces of defamatory and damaging online content and litigated more than 350 cases in 26 states and five countries.

Standout capability: Legal action. When false content won’t come down through outreach or platform policies, Minc Law can send demand letters and pursue defamation claims. It can also work to unmask anonymous posters.

Best for: Cases where the source behind a harmful AI answer is defamatory and needs a legal remedy. It pairs well with a removal-focused reputation firm: legal pressure on one side, removal and AI reputation work on the other.

What they do: Birdeye is a review and customer experience platform for multi-location brands. Its Birdeye AI Search product tracks brand and location-level visibility across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Google AI Overviews, Google AI Mode, Claude and Grok.

Standout capability: Location-level AI visibility scoring, citation tracking and sentiment analysis, tied to its review management tools.

Best for: Franchises and multi-location brands that want to monitor AI visibility location by location and keep review volume up.

Keep in mind: Birdeye is software. It can show you a negative source and help you publish better content. But it doesn’t remove third-party articles, records or posts.

What they do: Yext manages business listings and brand data across search engines, maps and directories. In March 2025 it launched Yext Scout, an AI search and competitive intelligence agent that tracks how brands appear across ChatGPT, Gemini, Perplexity, Grok and Google.

Standout capability: Keeping business facts accurate and consistent everywhere AI tools look, with competitor benchmarking built in.

Best for: Enterprise and multi-location brands whose main AI problem is inconsistent or outdated business information.

Keep in mind: Yext focuses on data you control, like listings and web content. It isn’t built to remove negative content published by others.

What they do: Podium is a customer communication platform for local businesses that combines messaging, review requests and payments. Its AI Employee handles lead response and appointment booking around the clock.

Standout capability: Generating a steady flow of fresh, positive reviews, which feed the review sites AI tools pull from when they describe local businesses.

Best for: Local service businesses such as auto dealers, home services, dental and medical practices that want more reviews and faster customer response.

Keep in mind: Podium builds positive signals. It doesn’t track AI answers directly or remove harmful content.

What they do: Vendasta is a white-label software platform for agencies and resellers that serve small businesses. Its reputation management platform monitors reviews across more than 100 sites and uses an AI agent to post personalized review replies.

Standout capability: White-label delivery, so agencies can offer review and reputation tools under their own brand.

Best for: Marketing agencies that want to add reputation services for many small business clients at once.

Keep in mind: Vendasta is a toolset for agencies, not a removal service, and its focus is reviews rather than AI answers.

What they do: Profound is an answer engine optimization (AEO) analytics platform that shows brands how often AI models mention them and in what context, across ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini and Google AI Overviews. The company raised $180 million at a $1.8 billion valuation in September 2026.

Standout capability: Large-scale measurement of AI share of voice and citation patterns for enterprise marketing teams.

Best for: Enterprise marketing and SEO teams that want detailed data on how their brand performs in AI answers compared with competitors.

Keep in mind: Profound measures and optimizes visibility. It doesn’t handle reputation crises or remove harmful content.

AI visibility and LLM reputation management is quickly replacing page-one rankings as the measure of how people see you. Monitoring platforms can tell you what AI says, and review tools can build positive signals. But changing a harmful answer means removing what it’s built on.

For anyone comparing the best companies for AI reputation management, that’s the deciding question: can they change the answer, or only report it? On that test, Reputation Resolutions ranks first.

#3199. iOS 27.2 adds new features in six iPhone apps, details here

iOS 27.2 recently launched with new features for iPhone users, including improvements across six Apple apps. Here’s what’s new.

One of my favorite additions to Messages this year, Suggested Actions, debuts in iOS 27.2.

Suggested Actions appear underneath messages in a conversation when relevant. They can suggest creating a calendar event or reminder, adding to a note, and more based on the context of the message.

The feature was originally part of the iOS 27 beta this summer, but didn’t make the public build. Now it’s back in iOS 27.2, new and improved. There’s also an option to fine-tune which types of suggestions you’ll see.

Read more: iOS 27.2 adds new Messages feature that’s already a favorite

Every major streaming service has its own profiles feature, letting users on the same account keep their viewing history and recommendations separate. Apple TV has long offered such a feature in tvOS, but now with iOS 27.2 and iPadOS 27.2 it’s coming to iPhone and iPad too.

When you launch the TV app in iOS 27.2, you’ll be greeted by a new profile selection screen. You can easily disable it if you don’t want to see if again. But if you ever share your iPhone with kids, the new profiles feature should come in handy.

Read more: iOS 27.2 gives Apple TV a new profiles feature on iPhone

Dual Capture is one of FaceTime’s best new features in years. Added in iOS 27, on compatible iPhones it lets you keep your front and rear cameras both active at the same time while on a FaceTime call.

iOS 27.2 brings a key upgrade to Dual Capture: it’s now available for Group FaceTime calls.

To use the feature, just hit the flip camera button like usual, and by default on iPhone 17 and newer you’ll stream both camera feeds simultaneously.

Read more: iOS 27.2 makes FaceTime’s best new feature even better

Timed with its new Home products push, Apple adds a pair of new Home app features in iOS 27.2 for compatible smart locks.

‘Lock After Closing’ is a new automation setting that lets you choose how long after a door is closed that it should lock automatically. Previously you could only set a duration based on the time since a door was unlocked, not closed.

‘Door Left Open’ tackles a related, but distinct problem: a door being left open too long. With compatible locks, you can configure the Home app to automatically notify you if a door has been left open for a certain period of time.

Read more: iOS 27.2 has three new changes just added this week

Apple Podcasts keeps getting better, with AI-powered automatic chapters and transcripts some of my favorite features. And in iOS 27.2, Apple has a welcome change to the Up Next queue on the Home tab.

Up Next is now split into two separate queues: New Episodes and Continue Playing.

Without the redesigned Health app, none of the new features appeal to me all that much. But performance improvements, bug fixes, and security fixes are always welcomed. What most of really wants is faster and more reliable Siri AI, along with support for a wider range of personal data, such as PDF documents on the iCloud Drive.

New Episodes contains only the latest episodes from shows you follow, while Continue Playing is a hub for all the episodes you’ve previously started but haven’t yet finished.

Apple’s Games app introduces some small updates in iOS 27.2 as well.

The Home tab now shows you recently downloaded games that you haven’t yet played. Previously, you would only see games with some play activity. And Apple says achievement progress and leaderboard scores have been updated in the Home tab to be easier to track. Finally, the Friends tab “provides context on friend suggestions and shows recent games played on friends’ player pages” per Apple.

Which new iOS 27.2 features are you most excited about? Let us know in the comments.

Electronic products now pack circuits, structures, thermal paths, and packaging into very small spaces. These physical domains interact with one another. A packaging choice can change how a shock load reaches a circuit board. Such interactions are hard to predict. Most are found during physical qualification, late in development. At that stage, the design is mostly fixed. A failure leads to redesign, rebuilds, and retesting. Physical tests give strong evidence of robustness, but they give limited insight into load paths and failure margins. Traditional simulation gives more detail, but it needs specialist skills and long manual setup. This white paper explains how guided virtual validation brings shock and drop assessment into the design phase. It reviews common test configurations, model inputs, and acceptance criteria. A packaged drop case study then shows how packaging can be optimized across all drop orientations and checked against physical test results.

#3196. Web Summit returns Thursday with rescheduled sessions after storm cancellation

Organisers promise their busiest closing day ever after the storm washed out the entire Wednesday programme.

Web Summit’s main stage in Lisbon in November 2025

Web Summit will return on Thursday for its final day, after Storm Charles forced the cancellation of the entire Wednesday programme at Europe’s biggest tech conference in Lisbon.

Organisers confirmed the restart in an email to attendees on Wednesday, promising “our busiest Thursday ever” with more speakers and meetups than any previous closing day. Many of the sessions lost to the storm have been moved to Thursday, and an updated schedule is expected later today.

Web Summit is officially back on tomorrow – Thursday, November 12 – for our final day.

It will be our busiest Thursday ever with more speakers and more meetups than ever before – with many rescheduled from Wednesday.

Keep an eye on the schedule later today for updates.

The decision to scrap day two came after Portugal’s government advised organisers that the programme should not go ahead.

Officials pointed to the risk of tidal flooding, severe public transport disruption, and high winds battering outdoor structures at the Parque das Nações venue.

That advice followed consultations with ANEPC, the country’s civil protection authority, and the Public Security Police. Organisers told attendees on Tuesday evening that their safety was the top priority and that affected ticket holders would be contacted directly.

Lisbon mayor Carlos Moedas had signalled the move hours earlier, saying “everything indicates” the event could not run on Wednesday. More than 60,000 people were at the venue this week, he said in comments reported by The Irish Times.

The storm’s reach extended well beyond the conference halls. Portugal declared a state of alert across the mainland for Wednesday, closing schools and non-essential public services, while Lisbon shut tunnels, parks, gardens, and cultural venues from midnight, The Portugal News reported.

IPMA, the national weather service, forecast gusts of up to 120km/h.

Attendees returning on Thursday will have plenty to catch up on, including the findings of the event’s tech industry survey, in which 60% of respondents said AI had increased their workload.

#3194. Spotify’s AI DJ adds nine voices and a setting to reduce interruptions

Spotify today expanded customization options for its AI DJ, allowing users to choose between different voices and personalities, as well as control how much the DJ talks between songs. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with Spotify’s AI DJ feature, the company describes it as “a personalized mix of music and commentary to help you discover new favorites and connect more deeply with the artists you love,” adding that it takes your listening history into account to “[bring] together your favorite tracks, songs you haven’t heard in years, and new releases to keep things feeling fresh.”

Spotify first introduced the interactive version of DJ in May 2025, and soon expanded its capabilities to Spanish-speaking users. Then, last May, Spotify expanded availability to more than 75 countries, alongside support for French, German, Italian, and Brazilian Portuguese.

Now, as spotted by TechCrunch, Spotify is introducing more customization options, including new voices and personalities, as well as the ability to reduce commentary between songs.

In a new post published on Spotify’s For the Record blog, the company announced today that “Spotify Premium listeners in markets where DJ is available can choose from an expanded selection of DJ voices in English and Spanish,” with seven new English options spanning British, American, Irish, Australian, and Indian accents, along with two new Spanish voices.

Additionally, Spotify now lets users choose whether they want commentary between sets of songs through a toggle that reduces the DJ’s interruptions to brief acknowledgments when starting a session or requesting different music.

#3193. California sinks its billionaire tax as a Brin-backed wealth tax ban leads

Opponents of the billionaire tax raised about 10 times as much as its backers. A second measure from their committee, barring new wealth taxes, is ahead in the count.

California voters have rejected Proposition 40, a one-time tax on the wealth of the state’s billionaires. The Associated Press called the race on Monday. California was still counting mail ballots nearly a week after the 3 November election.

The measure would have charged 5% on the net worth of residents worth more than $1bn. It would have been the first tax of its kind in the US, the AP reported. About 53% of voters opposed it with around 83% of the estimated vote counted, Laurel Rosenhall reported for The New York Times.

Google co-founder Sergey Brin gave $102m to Building a Better California, the committee that led the opposition, according to state campaign filings. The committee raised more than $333m, nearly a third of it from Brin, the AP reported. TNW reported in July that tech billionaires had already put $120m into defeating it.

Brin and fellow co-founder Larry Page started cutting ties with California before the vote, according to the AP. Brin is back at Google, working on Gemini. Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg said he would stay in the state for eight years. He also made a share deal with Meta to help him pay the tax without losing his stake. Some Meta shareholders have sued to block that plan.

The tax lost statewide even though San Francisco and Los Angeles counties backed it, Fortune reported. Santa Clara County, home to much of Silicon Valley, voted against it.

The SEIU United Healthcare Workers West union put the tax on the ballot. Most of the money would have replaced federal healthcare funding cuts. The union put the state’s loss at about $100bn over five years. Another 10% would have gone to education and food assistance. Backers said they could return with a new tax in 2028.

“Buying an election is not the same as winning the debate,” the measure’s proponents said in a statement on Monday.

Governor Gavin Newsom opposed the tax and warned it would drive the richest residents out of the state. He supports a national minimum tax on anyone worth more than $100m, the AP reported. A coalition that included Planned Parenthood and the California Medical Association also campaigned against it.

“Proposition 40 was a reckless experiment conducted on our state’s economy with little regard for the harms it would cause,” the coalition said in a statement.

The AP Voter Poll found that most voters under 30 backed the tax. Roughly 7 in 10 voters aged 65 and over voted against it.

Building a Better California also sponsored Proposition 42, which was ahead with 51.6% of the vote on 10 November, Molly A. Wallace reported for Fortune. The constitutional amendment bars new state taxes on personal property, including business interests, intellectual property and financial assets. It also blocks most taxes that apply retroactively. A third measure, Proposition 41, failed.

Opponents of the billionaire tax argued that voting for Proposition 42 would protect middle-class retirement savings from future taxes, the Times reported. If it passes, a new wealth tax in California would first need voters to undo it, Fortune reported.

In the same election, US voters rejected AI data centres in 40 of 41 local ballot measures.

#3192. Apple to investigate accident that killed three workers at iPhone parts factory in India

Reuters reports that three contract workers died after inhaling gas during an inspection at a Tata Electronics factory that produces iPhone components in India. Here are the details.

As frequent 9to5Mac readers probably know, Apple’s supply chain in India relies heavily on Tata, which manufactures iPhone components and accounts for a significant share of the country’s iPhone assembly operations.

Since Apple began diversifying its manufacturing operations away from China, India has emerged as a major production hub, with roughly a quarter of the world’s iPhones now manufactured in the country.

Earlier this year, Apple found itself linked to an environmental controversy in India, after the Tamil Nadu Pollution Control Board investigated allegations that wastewater from a Tata facility had contaminated nearby farmland water.

A few weeks later, however, Tata said the regulator had dropped further action against the facility after the company addressed the concerns raised.

At the time, Tata said it had ordered separate testing related to the facility and that the results supported its position that the plant was operating within the rules.

However, the matter was apparently not fully resolved, as just three days later, Reuters reported that local health officials were still investigating complaints from nearby farmers.

And while there had been no major developments reported about the wastewater investigation since then, Reuters reported today that three contract workers died in an accident at the same Tata facility.

The three contract workers died during maintenance work on an effluent treatment ​plant operated by Nalco Water at the Tata facility, which is located in Hosur in Tamil Nadu, ​district official Dinesh Kumar said, adding that the deaths occurred when the workers inhaled gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank.

Reuters added that “Apple’s team is visiting ​the plant to assist in ​the ongoing investigation,” though the company did not respond when reached for comment.

The report added that Tata and Tamil Nadu authorities are also investigating the fatal accident, and noted that “production was not affected as the facility was closed for the Hindu festival of Deepavali this week.”

To read Reuters’ full report, follow this link.

#3191. CleanupBuddy 2.0 expands beyond the keyboard with new display cleaning features

Developer Gui Rambo updated CleanupBuddy today, expanding its ability to prevent accidental inputs while cleaning your Mac from the keyboard to the touchscreen. Here are the details.

If you’re not familiar with CleanupBuddy, this is a nice little app that locks the keyboard to prevent accidental inputs while the user cleans it up.

Once they’re done cleaning, users can press and hold both Cmd keys to unlock the keyboard, then proceed to grease it up again.

The app also features a fun little animated character that reacts to your cleaning sessions with playful (and sometimes snarky) comments.

Today, CleanupBuddy was updated to version 2.0, with options to dim the display and ignore touch inputs, making it useful for users of both the new touchscreen MacBook Pro and Macs with traditional displays.

You can use the new “Lock Touch Screen” option to block touch input while cleaning a supported touch screen. On Macs without a touch screen, the “Dim Display” option can still be used to darken the display for easier cleaning.

Today’s update also tweaks the in-app character, which now uses on-device Apple Intelligence to generate personalized comments before and after cleaning sessions, based on stats such as time spent cleaning, key presses, and mouse clicks.

Rambo explains that these stats are collected only during cleaning sessions and stored locally on the Mac, and that users can independently turn off both cleanup stats and Apple Intelligence integration in the app’s settings.

Other tweaks in today’s update include temporarily disabling Sticky Keys and its Shift-key shortcut during cleaning sessions, as well as improving the readability of the “Start Cleanup” button when using Liquid Glass.

CleanupBuddy 2.0 is available for $2.99 and is compatible with macOS 14 and later, while the new personalized messages require macOS 26 or later, with Apple Intelligence enabled and its models ready to use.

To learn more about CleanupBuddy, follow this link.

#3190. iFixit tears down touchscreen MacBook Pro, reveals light-up Apple logo details

iFixit published its teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display today, revealing interesting details about how Apple brought back its illuminated logo on the lid. Watch it below.

iFixit’s teardown of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display is now live, and it explores not only how the new illuminated Apple logo works, but also its tandem OLED and how Apple managed to trim its weight down to 3 pounds (1.38 kg) from 3.4 pounds (1.55 kg) on the standard 14-inch model.

The teardown opens with a close look at the tandem OLED, which stacks two light-emitting layers to deliver higher brightness than conventional single-layer OLED displays.

Under a microscope, iFixit found that the blue subpixels are larger than the red and green ones, which they say should help reduce strain on the materials and potentially extend the display’s lifespan.

Most of the teardown process is quite familiar from past models, though iFixit noted that replacing the USB-C ports or fans still requires removing the entire logic board, despite both components being independently replaceable.

iFixit noted that the headphone jack also requires logic board removal, while the HDMI port, SDXC port, RAM, and storage remain soldered to the board.

As with past teardowns, iFixit also tested what happens when swapping logic boards between two MacBooks.

While last year’s M5 MacBook Pro failed to complete Touch ID calibration through Apple’s Repair Assistant, iFixit noted that the new model successfully recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor after a logic board swap, with True Tone, brightness controls, and the touchscreen all working as expected.

iFixit was also able to enroll a fingerprint with the donor board installed from another MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display.

As for the illuminated Apple logo, iFixit had a bit of a rough time getting to it, destroying the OLED panel in the process and even asking whether anyone had managed to remove it intact.

Once inside, iFixit found that the Apple logo is illuminated by a strip of four LEDs, which work in conjunction with a reflective layer and a diffuser to distribute the light evenly.

The Apple logo itself, in turn, has a two-way mirror coating that gives it a shiny, reflective appearance when the LEDs are off, while allowing light to pass through when they’re on.

When it comes to weight, Apple shaved 92 grams off the chassis and 101 grams off the display assembly, despite adding touch and an illuminated logo. The battery is just 2 grams lighter, while the slightly smaller trackpad saves another 8 grams.

Finally, iFixit gave the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR Display a repairability score of 5 out of 10. That was one point higher than last year’s M5 MacBook Pro, but one point below the cheaper MacBook Neo.

#3189. Top Wall Street analysts like these 3 dividend stocks for solid returns

The Federal Reserve indicated the possibility of a rate hike this year after its latest meeting, which could have implications for income-seeking investors.

Given this backdrop, dividend-paying stocks with strong yields and upside potential could help investors earn attractive returns.

Backed by solid research, top Wall Street analysts can provide key insights to pick stocks having the ability to generate compelling capital appreciation and pay consistent dividends, driven by solid fundamentals.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Kinetik is a midstream company operating in the Delaware basin. With a quarterly dividend of 81 cents per share (annualized dividend of $3.24 per share), KNTK stock offers a dividend yield of about 7%.

RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Kinetik stock and increased her price target to $53 from $50, citing expected growth from the KL2 project and sour gas opportunity in New Mexico. Scotto updated her estimates to reflect Kinetik's Q1 2026 results, with adjusted EBITDA beating estimates, driven by improved margins and Gulf Coast marketing gains that offset Waha price-related shut-ins.

The five-star analyst expects the Waha price-related shut-ins to persist until incremental takeaway capacity comes online later this year. Scotto said that Kinetik is well-positioned to capture New Mexico sour gas growth prospects when prices support activity. She sees the Northern Delaware Basin in New Mexico as a major growth opportunity for Kinetik. Scotto highlighted that Kinetik has purpose-built its system for sour gas handling, giving it an edge over new competitors that may face permitting delays of at least three years to build acid gas injection wells.

Additionally, Scotto pointed out Kinetik's attractive capital return framework, which targets a 3.5x to 4.0x leverage ratio, 3% to 5% hike in annual dividend until dividend coverage reaches 1.6x, and opportunistic share buybacks.

"We still view KNTK as a logical takeout candidate for buyers seeking to increase equity NGL barrels and sour gas processing," said Scotto.

Scotto ranks No. 211 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been successful 68% of the time, delivering an average return of 16%. See Kinetik Financials on TipRanks.

Oilfield services company SLB (SLB), formerly known as Schlumberger, is this week's second dividend pick. The company announced a quarterly cash dividend of nearly 30 cents per share, payable on July 9. At an annualized dividend of $1.18 per share, SLB stock offers a dividend yield of 2.5%.

Recently, Goldman Sachs analyst Neil Mehta reiterated a buy rating on SLB stock with a price target of $63, saying that he believes the company is "positioned to capitalize on long-term opportunities in oilfield activity globally triggered by the ongoing disruptions and shifting supply dynamics in the Middle East."

The five-star analyst expects SLB's dominant position in the international oilfield services market to bolster its earnings power over the long term, supported by increased activity levels over the medium to long term.

Given management's commentary on accelerated exploration activity in regions such as Latin America, Africa and Asia, and his expectation for accelerated final investment decisions in deepwater projects in West Africa, the Gulf of America and Brazil, Mehta expects SLB to benefit from higher services activity needed amid increasing drilling and production.

Furthermore, Mehta expects portfolio diversification from the Digital business and data center growth to drive higher earnings over the long term. Notably, the analyst expects SLB to deliver margins of about 40% in the Digital business this year, with further expansion in the years ahead.

Mehta ranks No. 626 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 60% of the time, delivering an average return of 10.7%. See SLB AI Stock Analysis on TipRanks.

Finally, moving on to tech giant IBM (IBM). The company is increasingly focusing on quantum computing and artificial intelligence to drive future growth. At a quarterly dividend of $1.69 per share, IBM stock offers a dividend yield of 2.7%.

Following a fireside chat with Ric Lewis, senior vice president of infrastructure at IBM, Bank of America analyst Wamsi Mohan reaffirmed a buy rating on IBM stock and increased his price target to $315 from $300.

The five-star analyst noted that Lewis views IBM Infrastructure as an increasingly less cyclical and more structurally advantaged business, with AI driving additional demand across the entire technology stack rather than only in graphics processing units.

Mohan added that AI tailwinds are most evident in IBM's Z mainframe offering, where program-to-program growth has increased from 110% several generations ago to the range of 120% to 125% in the prior cycle and roughly 135% for Z17. This acceleration is driven by AI workloads moving beyond fraud detection into inferencing areas like insurance, actuarial modeling, and transaction-level intelligence.

The analyst noted that IBM is benefiting from customers upgrading their systems and increased revenue from higher-value workloads from its existing customer base. Mohan also noted other positives like AI-led demand in IBM's storage business and the quantum roadmap.

"Overall, the fireside reinforced that IBM's Infrastructure business is positioned to compound through a combination of accelerating Z demand, AI-driven workload expansion, storage strength, and better monetization across a differentiated full-stack architecture," said Mohan.

Mohan ranks No. 21 among more than 12,300 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 65% of the time, delivering an average return of 52.6%. See IBM Insider Trading Activity on TipRanks.

#3187. Home Depot vs. Uber: One Stock Is Betting on a Housing Recovery, the Other on the Future of Transportation. Which Is the Better Buy for 2027?

Strong earnings growth, attractive valuations, and an uncertain economic outlook are creating two very different opportunities for investors heading into 2027.

Home Depot (HD -0.69%) and Uber Technologies (UBER -1.57%) are two market leaders facing very different challenges heading into 2027. Home Depot is navigating a prolonged housing slowdown, while Uber continues to deliver strong growth despite a struggling stock price and growing uncertainty about the future of autonomous transportation.

For investors, the distinction between temporary economic headwinds and potential long-term disruption could be critical in determining which stock offers the better opportunity in the upcoming year.

Home Depot is a home improvement retailer that serves homeowners, contractors, and construction professionals. The company has increasingly focused on expanding its professional contractor business through acquisitions to strengthen its presence in roofing, building materials, and specialty construction products. This strategy helps diversify revenue beyond traditional do-it-yourself home improvement spending.

In fiscal 2025, Home Depot generated $164.7 billion in revenue, an increase of 3.2% year over year. However, net income declined 4.4% to $14.2 billion as elevated borrowing costs and sluggish housing activity weighed on demand. More recent results highlight continued challenges. In the second quarter of fiscal 2026, revenue increased 5.7% to $47.9 billion, but comparable sales grew just 1.7%, indicating relatively modest underlying demand despite contributions from acquisitions.

Home Depot remains a substantial cash-generating business, producing approximately $12.6 billion in free cash flow during fiscal 2025. However, its debt-to-equity ratio of roughly 5.1x reflects a leveraged balance sheet, while its current ratio stood near 1.1x. Although its cash generation provides financial stability, meaningful growth will likely depend on an improvement in housing activity and renewed spending on larger renovation projects.

Uber operates a global mobility and delivery platform connecting millions of consumers with drivers, couriers, and merchants. The company is positioning itself for the transition to autonomous transportation, focusing on integrating self-driving vehicles into its existing network rather than developing its own autonomous driving technology. Management expects more than 2,000 fully driverless vehicles operating on its platform by the end of 2027.

In fiscal 2025, Uber generated $52 billion in revenue, an 18% year-over-year increase. Net income reached approximately $10.1 billion, although a substantial portion reflected a one-time tax benefit. More recent results highlight continued operating momentum. In the third quarter of 2026, gross bookings increased 20% to $59.8 billion, while revenue climbed 10% to $14.8 billion. Adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) rose 31% to nearly $3 billion, demonstrating improving profitability as the platform expands.

Uber also maintains a strong financial position. In fiscal 2025, the company generated $9.8 billion in free cash flow, an increase of 42% year over year. At the end of September 2026, it held approximately $10.1 billion in unrestricted cash and short-term investments, providing substantial flexibility to invest in new technologies and expand its operations.

Home Depot's biggest challenge remains the housing market. Elevated mortgage rates and sluggish home sales have weighed on renovation spending, while competition from other home improvement retailers adds pressure on pricing and margins. Although lower interest rates could eventually revive demand, a prolonged housing slowdown could continue limiting growth.

Uber faces a potentially more significant long-term challenge from autonomous transportation. While the company is positioning its platform to accommodate self-driving vehicles, competitors could increasingly offer rides directly to consumers, threatening Uber's market share and pricing power. Regulatory uncertainty surrounding driver classification, along with competition from Lyft (LYFT +1.55%) and other mobility providers, introduces additional risks.

Uber appears to offer better value based on future earnings estimates, though Home Depot remains the more affordable option when comparing its price to trailing sales.

Valuation metrics include sourcing from Financial Modeling Prep (FMP) and may differ from other data providers.

Home Depot and Uber offer two very different investment opportunities heading into 2027. The distinction comes down to the nature of their challenges. Home Depot's struggles are largely cyclical, meaning a recovery in housing activity could revive demand for home improvement projects. However, with mortgage rates remaining elevated and remodeling spending expected to grow modestly, a meaningful rebound may take time.

Uber, meanwhile, is already delivering strong operating results. Its latest quarterly gross bookings increased 20%, while adjusted EBITDA climbed 31%. Despite that momentum, the stock has struggled as investors question how autonomous vehicles could reshape its business. That uncertainty is legitimate, particularly as self-driving operators explore offering rides directly to consumers. However, Uber's established customer network, growing delivery business, and substantial cash generation provide competitive advantages as the industry evolves.

For investors looking toward 2027, Uber is my preferred buy. Trading at 20.4 times forward earnings compared with Home Depot's 23.3 times, Uber offers a compelling combination of faster growth and a slightly lower earnings valuation. Autonomous transportation poses meaningful long-term risks, but I believe the company's current operating momentum and financial strength make a stronger investment case than waiting for an uncertain housing recovery.

A post shared by Magnifique (@cookmagnifique)

I love my air fryer, but I also don't love that I have to switch appliances for certain meals. So, when I heard that Magnifique says, "No more swapping pots of appliances to put a crispy finish on the casserole," I was intrigued.

And thanks to its pure glass and stainless steel build with zero coatings, making it 100% non-toxic, you don't have to worry about chemicals or scratching it up when using it and scrubbing it clean.

But I always like to consider countertop space when looking at appliances like these. So, the big question for me is: how does it size up next to the Ninja Crispi? Well, it's a close one.

IEEE also bids farewell to innovators in space, power, and telecom

Bishnu Saroop Atal received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

Bishnu Saroop AtalAcoustics and signal processing pioneerLife Fellow, 93; died 19 August

Atal was an acoustics and signal processing researcher at Bell Labs in Murray Hill, N.J., and later at AT&T’s Shannon Laboratory, in Florham Park, N.J. His pioneering work on voice-coding techniques became the foundation for efficient, high-quality voice transmission over cellular networks. He received the 2013 IEEE Jack S. Kilby Signal Processing Medal for “fundamental and pioneering contributions to speech coding.”

He joined Bell Labs in 1961 as a communications researcher, and his early work there focused on speaker identification technology. During the 1960s he helped develop linear predictive coding, a powerful method for analyzing and compressing speech. LPC is now the most widely used method for encoding speech at a low bit rate.

Atal developed increasingly sophisticated low-bit-rate speech-coding techniques. They included multipulse LPC, which improved the quality of compressed speech.

He also worked with his colleague Manfred R. Schroeder to develop code-excited linear prediction, a method for producing high-quality speech at very low bit rates. CELP became a foundational technique in modern speech coding, letting digital communications systems carry voice using less bandwidth. The extra efficiency expanded cellular capacity, allowing wireless networks to handle more simultaneous calls.

Later in his career, he led the acoustics and speech research departments at Bell.

The company named him a Fellow in 1994. When AT&T Bell Laboratories split into separate research organizations in 1996, Atal continued his career at the AT&T Florham Park headquarters, and he was named a Fellow the following year.

He retired in 2002 and became an affiliate professor of electrical engineering at the University of Washington, in Seattle. There he continued his research in speech processing, speech recognition, and high-dimensional computing.

Atal was elected to the National Academy of Engineering in 1987 and the National Academy of Sciences in 1993. He received numerous awards including the 2018 International Speech Communication Association Medal for Scientific Achievement and a 2003 medal from the Franklin Institute.

He received a bachelor’s degree in physics in 1952 from the University of Lucknow, in India, and a master’s degree in 1955 in electrical engineering from the Indian Institute of Science, in Bengaluru. While working full time at Bell he earned a Ph.D. in EE in 1968 from the Polytechnic Institute of Brooklyn (now New York University’s Tandon engineering school), in New York City.

Darryl Palmer Jr.Chair of the IEEE Central Illinois SectionSenior member, 55; died 30 August

Palmer was a dedicated IEEE volunteer, serving as chair of the Central Illinois Section and as the government relations chair of Region 4. He was a member of the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society and its industrial activity committee. He also served as associate editor of the IEEE Transactions on Industrial Informatics.

In 1986, at age 16, Palmer completed a summer internship at NASA’s Glenn Research Center, in Cleveland. He helped develop FoilSim, an interactive educational software program that introduces aerodynamic engineering to preuniversity students.

While studying computer science at Cleveland State University in 1996, he joined the university’s Allen-Bradley PLC lab as a research assistant. He designed hardware and software systems for the Glenn Research Center to collect and process thermal wave imaging data. He also designed software for General Motors’ North American robotic and welding division.

In 1999 he completed a second internship at the research center and helped develop EngineSim, an educational software program that models jet engine design and testing.

For his work, NASA recognized him with a Space Act Award.

In 2000 he earned his bachelor’s degree in computer science and became a software engineer at the Danfoss Drives manufacturing facility in Loves Park, Ill. He worked on embedded control systems for variable-frequency drives and high-power equipment. He also developed sensorless control technology for beam pumps used in the oil and gas industry.

In 2014 Palmer and his wife, Alexandra “Sasha” Goodwin, founded Janus Choice, a health technology platform that matches hospital patients with post-acute care facilities. He served as its CEO until the company closed in 2020.

From 2018 to 2023, he was a lead software engineer at Adept Coalescence, a startup in Rockford, Ill., focused on developing front-end software for control systems. He then worked in Peoria, Ill., as a control systems team lead at Caterpillar, a manufacturer of construction and mining equipment.

Henry Leopold RichterTelecommunications engineerLife senior member, 99; died 12 August

Richter was a spacecraft engineer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, in Pasadena, Calif., before starting his own public safety communications consultancy.

He earned a bachelor’s degree and a Ph.D. at Caltech in 1952 and 1956, respectively. In 1955 he joined JPL as an engineer and supervisor of its new circuit elements group. Later, he was assigned to NASA’s Explorer program as project manager for satellite design, serving as a liaison between the organization’s satellite instrumentation group and its operations and data groups. Since 1958 the program has launched more than 90 missions for physics, geophysics, and astrophysics research.

As NASA prepared to launch Explorer 1 in January 1958, Richter worked with the San Gabriel Valley Radio Club in Los Angeles to set up stations across the United States to track the satellite.

He eventually was named JPL section chief and was responsible for scientific instruments on the lunar Ranger, Surveyor, and Mariner programs. He also helped develop NASA’s Deep Space Network, an international tracking and communications system.

Richter left NASA to become vice president and technical director of Xerox Electro-Optical Systems, in Pasadena, Calif.

In the mid-1970s, he joined the Los Angeles County Sheriff’s Department as a communications engineer, overseeing the department’s microwave and mobile radio networks.

He later ran a telecommunications consulting practice for more than 20 years. His clients included federal, state, and local government agencies, school districts, universities, and organizations. His work covered strategic technology planning and the design and implementation of public safety radio, microwave, CCTV, and paging systems.

He wrote several books including America’s Leap Into Space: My Time at JPL and the First Explorer Satellites (2015), a personal account of his experience working on the Explorer 1 and America’s space program.

In 2019 the Radio Club of America presented him with its Lifetime Achievement Award for “significant achievements and a major body of work that has advanced the art and science of wireless technology.”

Raymond L. GiordanoFormer RCA engineerLife member, 91; died 19 July

Giordano was an electrical engineer who designed integrated circuits and defense electronics at companies including Harris, Intersil, and RCA.

After earning his bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering in 1956 from the Newark College of Engineering (now the New Jersey Institute of Technology), Giordano joined RCA in Moorestown, N.J., as an engineer. He helped develop a video formatter for the company’s missile and surface radar division, and he taught in-house engineering courses, eventually attaining the rank of senior technical staff member.

Later he developed technologies for General Electric (which acquired RCA in 1986), Intersil, and Harris. He designed the circuitry for Kodak’s Cameo cameras and one of its laser printers.

Giordano was awarded several patents for his designs including a smoke detector chip for Siemens, a speed control chip for Ford, an engine control system for Delco Remy, and a control component for Chrysler.

He earned a master’s degree in EE in 1964 from the University of Pennsylvania, in Philadelphia.

Delano D. WilsonPresident of Power TechnologiesLife Fellow, 92; died 26 May

Wilson was president and CEO of Power Technologies, a consulting firm in Schenectady, N.Y., that specialized in electric power systems.

He was a director of R&D at General Electric in Schenectady until he joined Power Technologies in 1974 as a principal engineer. He developed utility systems and software for the company.

Wilson authored six books and 65 technical papers, and he held two patents.

Outside of his engineering work, he served on the boards of several hospitals, YMCAs, Rotary clubs, and chambers of commerce.

After returning to his hometown of Great Falls, Mont., in 1995, he volunteered as a court-appointed advocate, a trained community volunteer appointed by a judge to represent the interests of children in foster care.

Daniel I. Amey Jr.Electronic packaging engineerLife Fellow, 84; died 12 March

Amey was an electronic packaging engineer, working at several companies including General Dynamics, Sperry Univac, and E.I. du Pont de Nemours (now DuPont). His research interests included connectors, chip packages, and high-frequency materials.

He began his career in 1963 as an engineer in the General Dynamics electronics division, where he designed military electronic hardware including analog and digital support equipment for aerospace applications.

In 1967 he joined Sperry Univac in Blue Bell, Pa. From 1972 to 1981 he was engineering manager of packaging techniques, responsible for interconnection hardware for small and medium computer systems. His work focused on large-scale integration packages, hybrid circuits, connectors, and printed wiring board processes.

He left the company to serve as director of electronics technology at Thomas & Betts of Raritan, N.J. He led research and development of packaging and interconnection products there.

In 1986 he became a director of Elco, an electrical component manufacturer in Huntingdon, Pa., where he was responsible for the design and development of connector and packaging hardware.

In 1988 he joined E.I. du Pont de Nemours as director of its electronics and communications technology group in Research Triangle Park, N.C. He worked on packaging technology development, high-frequency materials characterization, and applications engineering. He retired from there as a research fellow.

Amey wrote or cowrote more than 70 technical papers and held more than 14 patents. He developed courses on electronic packaging and printed wiring technology for education companies McGraw-Hill and Cobblestone (formerly the Center for Professional Advancement).

He received the International Microelectronics Assembly and Packaging Society’s 2004 Wagnon Technical Achievement Award and the Electronic Industries Association’s 1984 Distinguished Engineering Contribution Award.

After receiving a bachelor’s degree in electrical engineering and a master’s degree in engineering science from Pennsylvania State University, he earned an MBA from Lehigh University, in Bethlehem, Pa.

Amanda Davis is a freelance writer based in San Diego.

#3183. Warren Buffett's Successor, Greg Abel, Just Bought $9.6 Billion of the Oracle of Omaha's Favorite Stock (No, Not Alphabet!)

Since mid-2018, Buffett and Abel have deployed roughly $92 billion of Berkshire Hathaway’s capital into a company near and dear to the Oracle of Omaha’s heart.

Few events garner more attention on Wall Street than Berkshire Hathaway's (BRKA +2.60%)(BRKB +1.41%) earnings reports. This is especially true now that Warren Buffett has retired and his successor, Greg Abel, is overseeing the company's day-to-day operations and its closely watched $359 billion investment portfolio.

While the September-ended quarter was more or less business as usual for the trillion-dollar conglomerate that Buffett built, with Berkshire recording $12.7 billion in operating earnings, another figure stole the show. Namely, a $9.6 billion purchase of the Oracle of Omaha's favorite stock by Abel.

The Oracle of Omaha's favorite stock is back on the menu. Image source: Getty Images.

Through the first half of 2026, Abel's headline buy was Google parent Alphabet (GOOGL -0.27%)(GOOG -0.38%). While Buffett initiated the position in Alphabet before his retirement, it was Abel who grew it into a top-three holding at one point. Berkshire's new boss has put tech on the menu in a way that wasn't seen under Buffett.

But it wasn't a tech purchase that raised eyebrows in the third quarter. In fact, you won't even find evidence of this purchase in Berkshire Hathaway's quarterly Form 13F, which should be filed on Nov. 16.

In Berkshire's third-quarter operating results, on the final page before the executive certifications, the company details Abel's purchase activity in the stock Buffett holds nearest and dearest to his heart... Berkshire Hathaway.

BREAKING: Berkshire Hathaway more than doubled its stock buybacks in Q3 2026, repurchasing $9.6 billion of its own shares. This brings total buybacks in 2026 to $14.4 billion, marking a sharp reversal after the company paused repurchases for nearly 22 months. Berkshire also revealed that it has been a net buyer of stocks in 2026, with net purchases hitting +$11.2 billion YTD. This compares to net stock sales of -$10.6 billion over the same period in 2025. Berkshire is deploying capital again.

Between July 1 and Sept. 30, Abel oversaw the purchase of 4,536 Class A shares (BRKA) and 12,384,959 Class B shares (BRKA), totaling approximately $9.6 billion. This more than doubles the $4.53 billion spent on share buybacks in the second quarter and brings cumulative share repurchases between Buffett and Abel since mid-2018 to approximately $92 billion.

As long as Berkshire Hathaway has at least $30 billion in combined cash, cash equivalents, and U.S. Treasury bills on its balance sheet -- it closed out September 2026 with $377.4 billion -- and Abel believes the company's shares are intrinsically cheap, buybacks can be made with no end date or ceiling.

Since Berkshire Hathaway doesn't pay a dividend, buybacks are a direct way to reward its shareholders (in case a greater-than-6,000,000% outperformance of the S&P 500 since the mid-1960s wasn't enough). Buybacks encourage the long-term investing ethos that Buffett values and can incrementally increase investors' ownership stakes over time.

A hearty share repurchase program can also make a company's stock more attractive to fundamentally-focused investors. Companies with steady or growing net income and a declining outstanding share count, courtesy of an ongoing buyback program, should see earnings per share rise over time.

An aggressive share buyback program can also signal to Wall Street and investors that management sees value in their company's stock.

BRK.A Price to Book Value data by YCharts

Over Warren Buffett's final 19 months as CEO, as well as during Abel's first two months at the helm, not one penny was used for buybacks. During this 21-month period, Berkshire's stock predominantly traded at a 60% to 80% premium to its book value. Since mid-2018, Berkshire's bosses have consistently green-lit buybacks when its shares trade at less than a 50% premium to book value. For context, shares have oscillated between a 40% and 50% premium over the previous two quarters.

Even though Buffett and Abel have been decisive net sellers of stocks over the last four years, Buffett's favorite stock is clearly on the menu.

Inside NASA’s open call for its next astronaut class: who qualifies and how to get your application in

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

NASA has formally opened applications for its next generation of astronaut candidates, kicking off a recruitment window aimed squarely at returning humans to the lunar surface, building an enduring presence at the Moon Base, and preparing for the first crewed expeditions to Mars.

With the agency's active astronaut corps currently standing at just 32 members, the newly selected class will step into rigorous training for spacewalking, lunar geology, and high-performance flight.

Here is a full breakdown of the eligibility criteria, experience thresholds, and how to submit your application before the December deadline.

Getting on NASA’s astronaut short-list is about having the right resume. You need U.S. citizenship and serious technical firepower. That usually means a master’s degree in a STEM field like engineering, computer science, or the hard sciences.

NASA also leaves the door open for high-level alternatives: two years into a technical PhD, a completed medical degree (like an MD, DO, PA, or DNP), or a diploma from a nationally recognized test pilot school paired with a STEM bachelor’s.

Once the degree is handled, you have to prove you can perform under pressure. Applicants need at least three years of real-world career hustle (doctors can count their residency). For aviators, flight hours substitute for office time — specifically, 750 command hours in high-performance jets, 1,500 hours in other planes (with half in command), or 1,000 helicopter hours.

If your paper credentials clear the bar, there’s one last hurdle: surviving NASA’s exhaustive physical exam and proving you have the calm communication and teamwork chops to live in a tin can with five other people.
