#3180. GrowGeneration (GRWG) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Store cuts and tariff refunds drove a profit swing as margins climbed sharply.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

GrowGeneration Corp. (GRWG -3.82%) reported a transition from a retail-centric hydroponic provider to a national commercial cultivation supply and proprietary brand platform. Management reduced its retail footprint to 19 stores during the third quarter and expects to operate 14 locations by the end of 2026, down from 65 locations in 2022. The company achieved its highest quarterly net income since 2021, supported by $2.6 million in tariff refunds and increased sales of internal brands. While total revenue declined slightly compared to the prior year, the company reported positive adjusted EBITDA for the second consecutive quarter and maintained a debt-free balance sheet with $41.8 million in liquidity.

Operator: Hello, everyone, and welcome to GrowGeneration's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. My name is Julie, and I will be your operator for today's call. [Operator Instructions] This conference call is being recorded, and a replay of today's call will be available on the Investor Relations section of GrowGeneration's website. I will now hand the call over to Phil Carlson with KCSA Strategic Communications for introductions and the reading of the safe harbor statements. Please go ahead, Phil.

Phil Carlson: Thank you, operator, and welcome, everyone, to GrowGeneration's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results Conference Call. With us today from GrowGeneration are Darren Lampert, Co-Founder and Chief Executive Officer; and Greg Sanders, Chief Financial Officer. The company's third quarter 2026 earnings press release was issued after close of market today. A copy of this press release is available on the Investor Relations section of the GrowGeneration website at ir.growgeneration.com. I would like to remind everyone that certain comments made on this call include forward-looking statements, which are subject to the safe harbor provisions of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 1995.

These forward-looking statements are based on management's current expectations and beliefs concerning future events and are subject to several risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those described in these forward-looking statements. Please refer to today's press release and other filings with the SEC for a detailed discussion of the risks that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied in any of the forward-looking statements made today. During the call, we'll use some non-GAAP financial measures as we describe business performance. SEC filing as well as the earnings press release, which provide reconciliations of non-GAAP financial measures to the most directly comparable GAAP measures are all available on our website.

Following prepared remarks, management will be happy to take your questions. [Operator Instructions]. Now I will hand the call over to GrowGeneration's Co-Founder and CEO, Darren Lampert. Darren, please go ahead.

Darren Lampert: Thanks, Phil, and good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for joining us to review GrowGeneration's third quarter 2026 financial results and to discuss our outlook for the remainder of the year. The third quarter represents another step in GrowGeneration's transformation into a commercial proprietary brand-driven business. We delivered net sales of $44.8 million, gross margins of 32.4% and $2.3 million of adjusted EBITDA. These results demonstrate our progress in fundamentally reshaping our business, strengthening our revenue quality and building a more efficient and profitable operating model. Over the past several years, we've expanded beyond our retail roots to serve commercial growers nationwide.

Three priorities have guided us, expanding our commercial sales team, growing sales of our proprietary brands and lowering the cost of serving customers by making better use of our distribution network. At the center of our transformation is the expansion of our commercial business. GrowGeneration has developed a national platform serving commercial cultivators across specialty agriculture and controlled environmental agriculture. Our competitive advantage is our cultivation expertise and a comprehensive portfolio of cultivation supplies. Proprietary brand sales grew approximately 19% year-over-year to $14.5 million, while surpassing 40% of cultivation and gardening net revenue for the quarter as we continue to see strong growth from our portfolio of brands.

We've also continued to consolidate locations and simplify our distribution network to lower the cost of serving growers. In the third quarter, store and other operating expenses fell approximately 12% year-over-year from $7.2 million to $6.4 million. During the quarter, we began the process of closing 2 additional stores, which was completed subsequent to quarter end. We expect to close another 2 to 3 locations before year-end, bringing our total fourth quarter closures to approximately 4 to 5 locations. These actions, together with targeted workforce reductions and other operational improvements are part of our broader restructuring plan to reduce fixed costs and improve operating efficiency.

We expect to complete the majority of these initiatives by the end of 2026, positioning GrowGeneration for greater profitability in the year ahead. Technology is another way we're increasing productivity and lowering costs. GrowGen Pro already gives our commercial and wholesale customers a convenient way to manage their accounts and place orders online. In October, we acquired technology from Order Junky to improve our sales team's efficiency. We're integrating tools that bring customer pricing, inventory availability and freight costs into a single quote that a sales rep can turn into an order without reentering the details. We're also evaluating the platform's AI capabilities can reduce routine administrative work.

For 2027, our goal is to give growers faster, more accurate quotes and make repeat purchases easier. We expect this will free our sales team to spend more time with customers and help us grow commercial sales without a corresponding increase in overhead. Turning to MMI Storage Solutions. The business generated $9.2 million in third quarter revenue, ahead of our expectations. MMI's performance through September has exceeded our initial expectations for 2026, and we're on track for strong year-over-year revenue growth for the full year. Looking ahead, we see opportunities to put MMI's engineering and manufacturing capabilities to work for more customers in industrial and specialty markets, expanding our business beyond cultivation.

The progress we're making is increasingly visible in our profitability. For the 9 months ended September 30, adjusted EBITDA improved to approximately $1 million from a loss of $4 million a year ago. We also reported our highest GAAP net income quarter since 2021. While the third quarter tariff recovery contributed to that improvement, we're continuing to focus on the underlying initiatives that will continue to drive our business to greater levels of profitability. We ended the quarter with $41.8 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities and no debt. That gives us flexibility to invest selectively in our commercial business, proprietary brands and technology.

During the quarter, we also returned approximately $1 million to shareholders through the repurchase of 700,000 shares at an average price of $1.46 per share. Given our progress to date and increased visibility, we are refining our full year revenue guidance to $163 million to $165 million from our original range of $162 million to $168 million. We're also taking further steps in the fourth quarter to strengthen profitability in 2027. With 4 to 5 additional store closures we plan to complete by year-end, along with other restructuring activities, we believe it is prudent to withdraw our previously full year adjusted EBITDA guidance.

And while these actions may create some near-term uncertainty, longer term, they will meaningfully lower our cost base and position the business for improved profitability in 2027. Looking ahead, our plan is to accelerate GrowGeneration's evolution into a leading national commercial cultivation supply and proprietary brand platform with multiple engines for profitable growth. To do that, we will prioritize expanding our proprietary brand penetration within our commercial customer base establishing deeper strategic relationships with commercial cultivators, expanding their operations and continuing to broaden MMI's customer base by entering additional verticals. Underlying all of this is our commitment to building a leaner, more efficient, technology-enabled organization.

We intend to leverage our national distribution infrastructure, commercial sales capabilities, proprietary brands and customer relationships to grow revenue while managing our cost structure. That concludes my remarks. Now I'll turn the call over to our CFO, Greg Sanders.

Greg Sanders: Thank you, Darren, and good afternoon, everyone. I'll begin with a review of our third quarter 2026 results, and then I'll provide additional context on our outlook for the rest of the year. We reported third quarter results that were consistent with our expectations and reflect the continuing transformation of GrowGeneration. Our results were characterized by strong proprietary brand sales in our cultivation and Gardening segment and continued growth and profitability in our Storage Solutions business. We delivered another quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA as well as a substantial year-over-year improvement in net income as we reported positive net income for the quarter.

For the third quarter of 2026, GrowGeneration reported net sales of $44.8 million compared to $47.3 million during the same period last year. Our revenue was in line with our guidance range and a slight decrease to 2025 due to a few large onetime transactions in the prior year period. Cultivation and Gardening segment net sales were $35.6 million for the quarter compared to $38.4 million in the same period last year. Proprietary brand sales represented 40.6% of Cultivation and Gardening revenue, up from 31.6% last year. Proprietary brand sales increased $2.3 million or 19.3% to $14.4 million for the quarter.

Through September, those sales grew $7.6 million or 23.4% to $40.1 million, offsetting the decline in third-party product sales and keeping total segment revenue slightly ahead of last year. Storage Solutions net sales were $9.2 million in the third quarter, up from $8.9 million a year ago and ahead of our expectations. Demand from retail and industrial customers contributed to the segment's performance. For the first 9 months of 2026, sales increased $2.2 million or 10.2% to $24 million, putting MMI ahead of our initial plan for the year. Gross profit increased $14.5 million compared to $12.9 million a year ago, and gross margin rose 520 basis points to 32.4% from 27.2%.

As anticipated, we recognized a $2.6 million benefit from IEEPA tariff refunds as a reduction in cost of sales. Cultivation and Gardening accounted for the increase in gross profit with segment gross profit up $1.7 million or 18.4%. In addition to the IEEPA refunds, a higher mix of proprietary brand sales helped margin. Lower sales from a smaller footprint for our stores weighed on gross profit, while pricing pressure, higher transportation costs and higher estimated inventory obsolescence costs weighed on margin. In Storage Solutions, gross profit dollars were essentially unchanged, although segment margin declined modestly. Turning to expenses. Total operating expenses declined 7.1% to $14.6 million from $15.7 million a year ago.

Store and other operating expenses fell 11.9% to $6.4 million from $7.2 million, reflecting our smaller store footprint. SG&A increased to $6.8 million from $5.7 million, driven by higher commercial sales-related spending and one-time charges incurred during the quarter. Depreciation and amortization totaled $1.2 million, down $1.5 million or 55.2% compared to $2.6 million in the same period last year. The decrease primarily reflects asset retirements related to cost reduction initiatives and certain intangible assets reaching the end of their useful lives. GAAP net income was $0.2 million, a $2.7 million improvement compared to a net loss of $2.4 million or negative $0.04 per share in the prior year period.

The improvement was primarily driven by higher gross margin, including the tariff refund benefit and lower operating expenses, partially offset by lower sales volume. In the third quarter, we delivered our second consecutive quarter of positive adjusted EBITDA. Non-GAAP adjusted EBITDA, as defined in our press release, was $2.3 million, a $1 million year-over-year improvement compared to $1.3 million in the prior year. Now turning to the balance sheet. We ended the quarter with $41.8 million of cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities and no debt. We continue to maintain a debt-free balance sheet. Our cash position gives us the financial flexibility to invest in organic growth, evaluate strategic opportunities and opportunistically return capital to shareholders.

We also returned approximately $1 million to shareholders during the quarter, repurchasing 700,000 shares at an average price of $1.46 per share, excluding transaction costs. We did so while preserving the liquidity we need to fund operations and invest in the business. At quarter end, approximately $8 million remained available for future repurchase. As Darren outlined, we are narrowing our full year revenue guidance to $163 million to $165 million. We are also withdrawing our previous adjusted EBITDA guidance of $2 million to $3 million due to the actions we are now taking to lower our ongoing cost base and position GrowGeneration for greater profitability in 2027.

While the store closures and other restructuring activities will affect our fourth quarter results, we expect the resulting savings and operating efficiencies to strengthen our financial performance in the year ahead. That said, we're satisfied with our third quarter results and with our performance through September, which was ahead of our initial plan for the year. We ended the quarter with $41.8 million in cash, cash equivalents, marketable securities and no debt. We have the financial flexibility to carry out our fourth quarter initiatives while continuing to invest in the business. We believe these actions position us to extend our multiyear track record of improving profitability heading into 2027.

With that, I'll turn the call back to Darren for closing remarks.

Darren Lampert: Thanks, Greg, and thank you again to everyone for joining us today. In closing, the most important takeaway today is that GrowGeneration is a fundamentally different business from what we were several years ago. We have substantially transitioned from a retail-centric hydroponic business into a national commercial cultivation supply and proprietary brand platform. We've expanded our proprietary brands, reduced operating expenses and improved profitability. And we've accomplished this while maintaining a strong balance sheet with no debt. Our third quarter results demonstrate the progress we've already made to building a stronger, more profitable company that generates sustainable cash flow and creates long-term value for our shareholders. I want to thank our employees, customers, vendors and stakeholders for their continued support.

That concludes our prepared remarks. Operator, please open the line for questions

Operator: [Operator Instructions] Your first question comes from Aaron Grey from Alliance Global Partners.

Aaron Grey: So first question for me, just if you could quantify the expected savings from the initiative expected to be completed in 2026. So how should we think about 2027 from a margin structure and profitability given that's what this initiative will be setting up for?

Greg Sanders: Yes. Thanks for the question, Aaron. So far, we're encouraged with the performance in 2026. We've brought the business from a $14 million adjusted EBITDA loss in '24 to a $6 million adjusted EBITDA loss last year and this year, we're at $1 million profit through the first 3 quarters. And we see an opportunity to reposition the business for heightened profitability next year. We are working through the restructuring plan right now. We intend to close 2 to 3 additional locations yet this quarter. We've already closed 2, so we're already underway. We are looking at other rationalizations across the company, including inventory charges that may occur in the fourth quarter.

So at this point, obviously, we dropped the EBITDA guidance with just the uncertainty around Q4 specifically, but we are aiming to complete most of the actions this quarter. There may be some additional actions that trail into the first quarter of 2027. Overall, we expect the resulting actions to meaningfully improve profitability in 2027. As we finalize our restructuring accounting, we will issue an 8-K with an update on how we see the incremental improvement translating into our results next year.

Aaron Grey: Okay. So if not able to quantify now, I guess, maybe taking it a different way, the stores that you are closing, the 4 to 5, those were weighing on the margin now. So getting out of those, and I know there might be some leases you might be able to get out as well. It's fair to say those were a drag on profitability currently and will be accretive once you get through the respective inventory of those stores, which might take 4Q into 1Q next year?

Darren Lampert: I think, Aaron, when you take a look at it, this will be -- we've closed 10 stores since the third quarter last year. Adding the additional 4 stores in the fourth quarter will be down 14 stores from Q3 last year. Each store closing certainly goes with cost savings, both from store employees, lease, and it funnels down to back-office staff and everything that goes into running these stores. When you start taking a look at the EBITDA guidance that we're giving where we started a couple of years ago, back in 2024, we lost about $16.5 million on an adjusted basis.

We lost $6 million last year and most likely going to be profitable this year or [ positive ] through the third quarter. So I think it's the whole show. You're talking about transportation, you're talking about distribution costs, you're talking about warehousing costs, inventory costs, inventory obsolescence costs. So I think when you take the whole picture as a whole and where we've come in the last couple of years going from $16 million in 2024 on the loss side to, again, we're positive $1 million this year right now. I think you can kind of look where the future is going.

We've been pretty transparent with Wall Street with the store closings and going to a B2B business, growing proprietary brands, which is over 40% right now and with margins increasing and expenses going down. So we are right now because everything is working, we're accelerating what we've been doing over the last 5 years. And I think this is probably one of the -- probably getting to the end of it. But what we're seeing right now is all positive. And so we're accelerating to get where we need to get.

Operator: Your next question comes from Brian Nagel from Oppenheimer.

Brian Nagel: So I think my question is going to be a follow-up to the prior question, but more -- maybe more qualitative. But with this -- the actions you're taking now in the fourth quarter, what spurred this? Is there something specific you saw in the business that caused you to take what seems to be more aggressive actions? And then I'll have a follow-up.

Darren Lampert: I think, Brian, a couple of different things. One, when changing business models from a retailer from a business to consumer to a business to business, there's certainly a lot to be done. And what we're seeing within the business right now is the business-to-business is working, the business-to-consumer is not. The traffic within the stores are just not there. So we're pretty much refining. We're changing the business as we've done over the last 5 years. There's nothing that is really pushing what we're doing right now. But as you know, costs are going up, transportation costs are going up, distribution costs are going up, container pricing are going up right now.

And I think we're just being very proactive, but we're being proactive into strength. The business is working. And we do believe that there's a lot of expenses that we can still take out of this business. And I think it starts with the stores. When you take the store business out within the store business, the purchasing team gets a little lighter. The supply chain gets lighter. Every component of the cost center of the business drops. And that's what we're working on right now. We were able to get rid of some leases. We paid to get out of some leases.

But when you look last year, as I said earlier, third quarter of 2025, we'll be down 14 stores from then. And you see it's not really impacting the -- you're not really impacting our sales nor our profitability. Our profitability is going up and our sales are pretty much staying the same. And I think we've been pretty transparent that we close stores, we do lose a bunch of walk-in business. we're picking up on the commercial side, and we're picking it up on our proprietary brand side and also our wholesale side. So most of the business is working. The stores are not.

Brian Nagel: That's very helpful, Darren. So I guess just a clarification on that. So as we think about the actions you're taking here in the fourth quarter, that's primarily more aggressively closing a larger number of stores?

Darren Lampert: Again, we're going from -- I think we're going from 19 down to 14. So on a percentage basis is a pretty high number. We still do use some stores for distribution. You'll probably see another couple of store closings next year, but they won't be -- you won't see 5 in 1 quarter. When you go back to last year, we closed, I think, 7 in the third quarter last year and 4 in the fourth quarter last year. So we've been closing pretty quickly. We started with 65 stores back in 2022. So we'll be down from 65 stores down to 14 by the end of this year.

Brian Nagel: Okay. And then my final question, just with regard to the guidance. So it sounds like you're going to have -- you'll have -- if I'm understanding correctly, you'll have extra expenses now in this fourth quarter given these restructuring actions. So when you report fourth quarter results, will you be able to basically articulate how much of the results are kind of one-time in nature, reflecting these more aggressive restructuring actions versus the ongoing operations of the business?

Greg Sanders: Yes, that's exactly right, Brian. Our aim with this action that we're taking in the fourth quarter, it may extend slightly into the first as well is to quantify the total impact and include the forward-looking guidance in 2027 reflective of the improvements that we believe we can make and execute in this window of time to better position the company for that continued track record of improved profitability that we've delivered the last several years into 2027 and beyond.

Operator: Your next question comes from Mark Smith from Lake Street.

Mark Smith: Curious, first off, just as we continue to transition more to B2B business here, any call-outs on customer concentration or increased risk that you run there?

Greg Sanders: I was going to say we -- as a company, Mark, and it's a very good question, are still very diversified from a customer perspective. There are no customers in our portfolio that account for more than 5% of sales today. When we close stores, we aim to retain all of the commercial customers that shop in that general market or region through another closely approximated store or through our commercial sales team. So from a concentration perspective, we feel that these moves don't present a significant amount of risk from a retention perspective given the diversified nature of our customer base across the portfolio.

Mark Smith: Okay. And then just curious if you can give us just an update on your view of the industry and if you've seen any kind of tailwinds develop as we've moved into rescheduling?

Darren Lampert: I think right now, Mark, it's going to be some time and people are still awaiting rescheduling on adult use still in front of the ALJ and people are expecting a decision within -- hopefully within -- by the end of the year, but which keeps getting pushed back. But I think people are still waiting. Our business has been relatively strong. Again, we've closed 14 stores. It will be 14 stores in the last year, and we do lose business when we close stores. So if you took the store closures out, we'd have quite an increase year-over-year on a sales basis.

But again, we're certainly making that back on the other side of it by cutting expenses and growing proprietary brands. Our proprietary brands were up 19% year-over-year in a difficult market. So we believe you'll see a lot of consolidation on an ongoing basis. And the larger customers want to deal with a company that can handle their needs from a financing side, from a product side of it and others from a technical side of it. We have built a pretty incredible technical team at GrowGen and a commercial sales team at GrowGen. And it is certainly helping keep the customers as we close stores.

And one of the main -- when we take a look at what stores we're closing, it's the stores that have mostly commercial customers that we can service with our commercial team and service through drop shipping from our warehouses. It's not the stores that have -- that still do have customer walk-ins. So we do still have a number of stores where the -- where customers are coming to the stores, shopping at the stores. Those stores we will keep for a while. There's no reason to close some of them. We still do have some profitable stores within the portfolio.

But the other side is when we close stores, we are getting rid of back-office staff and really cutting down the expenses of this company. I think you guys will be quite happy when you hear what we've done within the fourth quarter on really trimming expenses of this company really without trimming sales forecast for next year. So we're excited to go into 2027, and we certainly hope cleaner than we've gone into any other year since 2021.

Operator: There are no further questions at this time. I will turn the call back over to Darren for closing remarks.

Darren Lampert: Thank you. I want to once again thank our employees, customers, vendors and stakeholders for their continued support in GrowGeneration. I want to wish everybody a happy holiday season, and we look forward to updating everybody with our fourth quarter and year-end numbers in March. And hopefully, we'll have some news out before then. Thank you.

Operator: Ladies and gentlemen, this concludes today's conference call. You may now disconnect. Thank you.

#3179. End of an era: Apple Support Community forums will permanently close on November 20

Users visiting the Apple Support Community tonight were greeted with a message informing them that the platform will permanently shut down on November 20. Here are the details.

If you have ever had a question or ran into a problem with an Apple product, chances are you have come across the Apple Support Community, the company’s official discussion forums where users from around the world help each other troubleshoot issues and share tips.

The platform has a history dating back to at least 1998, when it was known as Apple Tech Exchange. Since then, it was renamed Apple Discussions before relaunching as Apple Support Communities in April 2011, with a redesigned interface, personalized profiles, and a reputation system that rewarded users for helping others.

Tonight, however, users who tried to access the platform were greeted with the following message:

The AppleCare Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state.

You can continue to find trusted guidance and support on the official Apple Support site.

We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products.

Right now, the portal still shows a “Sign in” button, though it leads only to an AppleConnect login page labeled “AC Communities Web – Internal,” suggesting that access is now restricted to Apple employees.

Interestingly, Apple’s message refers to the “AppleCare Support Community,” rather than the “Apple Support Community,” which is how the platform is officially branded.

Still, the forums are already in read-only mode, with users able to browse existing discussions, search for answers, and interact with posts through the “Me too” and voting buttons, but no longer submit new questions or replies.

At the time of writing, the most recent post was published just 57 minutes earlier, suggesting that Apple only recently disabled new submissions.

9to5Mac has reached out to Apple for comment and clarification on the scope of the shutdown, and we’ll update this story if we hear back.

Few things beat settling in with a juicy period drama, and "The Gilded Age" never fails to deliver all the extravagant costumes, forbidden romances, and social squabbles that'll have you hooked. Set in New York City during the 1880s, it follows New York’s upper crust trying desperately to climb the ranks of the rich and famous.

#3177. Precipio (PRPO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Precipio targets a $40 million run rate by 2027 as it expands its sales team.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Precipio, Inc. (PRPO +6.53%) reported third-quarter results characterized by a transition from achieving financial independence in 2025 toward a strategy of accelerated revenue growth for 2027. Management reported that the company achieved a quarterly cash balance exceeding $3.5 million while maintaining positive adjusted EBITDA and operating cash flow. The company stated its intent to leverage established distribution agreements with four major industry partners to scale its product division, targeting a combined annualized revenue run rate of $40 million by the end of 2027. This growth plan includes doubling the sales force and hiring a senior marketing executive to enhance clinical credibility and market awareness. Management noted that current facility infrastructure is already equipped to handle up to $100 million in annual revenue without further major capital expenditures.

Operator: Welcome to Precipio Q3 2026 Shareholder Update Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] Please note that the conference is being recorded. Statements made during this call contain forward-looking statements about our business. You should not place undue reliance on forward-looking statements as these statements are based upon our current expectations, forecasts and assumptions and are subject to significant risks and uncertainties. These statements may be identified by words such as may, will, should, could, expect, intend, plan, anticipate, believe, estimate, predict, potential, forecast, continue or the negative of these terms or other words or terms of similar meaning.

Risks and uncertainties that could cause our actual results to differ materially from those set forth in any forward-looking statements include, but are not limited to, the matters listed under Risk Factors in our annual report on Form 10-K for the year ended December 31, 2025, which is on file with the Securities and Exchange Commission as well as other risks detailed in our subsequent filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. These reports are available at www.sec.gov.

Statements and information, including forward-looking statements, speak only to the date they are provided, unless an earlier date is indicated, and we do not undertake any obligation to publicly update any statements or information, including forward-looking statements, whether as a result of new information, future events or otherwise, except as required by law. Now let me hand the call over to Ilan Danieli, Precipio's CEO. Please go ahead.

Ilan Danieli: Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Before we jump into a review of the results for Q3 2026 and share several thoughts for 2027, I thought that as we come to the end of another successful year, it might be helpful to add another member of the management team to these calls. I'd like to introduce my Co-Founder and Precipio's Chief Operating Officer, Zaki Sabet. Along with Dr. Ayman Mohamed, the 3 of us started Precipio in 2011, and we've been inseparable since. Prior to founding Precipio, Zaki spent his career in the diagnostics industry. While at college, Zaki worked as an accessioner during the night shift in a lab in New Jersey.

And over the years, he moved up through the ranks of lab tech then supervisor to eventually manage the entire laboratory. Bringing his in-depth expertise, Zaki was responsible for building what is today, to the best of our knowledge, at our size, one of the few profitable hematopathology laboratories in the country. At Precipio, Zaki oversees all company operations, including both our clinical laboratory as well as operations for the products division, including manufacturing and supply chain. Today, Zaki will be joining me in sharing some remarks, and then we'll also be available to answer questions during the Q&A section.

As this is our last scheduled shareholder call of 2026, I'd like to put these results in the context of the progress we've made over the past couple of years and explain how that progress sets the stage for 2027. In 2025, our focus was on getting the company to a cash flow positive position. We've gone through several dilutive financings and decided that it was time for the company to stand on its own 2 feet and become financially independent. So we set our eyes on reaching cash flow positive through a combination of revenue growth alongside significant operational efficiency improvements. And at the end of 2025, we were there.

Our company was cash flow positive, no longer dependent on outside capital in order to survive. And for the first time, we were able to respond to the calls from the various investment banks and hedge funds looking to provide capital to Precipio with a polite but clear, no thank you. I can tell you, as the person responsible for raising money to keep the lights on for 15 years, that was a wonderful moment. The second goal in 2025 was to determine if the products we created and that were used in our own lab would be real value to other laboratories.

We carefully explored this market by identifying target customers in several segments, which would serve as an indicator of market interest. This meant reaching a better understanding of which products in which configuration suited each segment. It meant continuously refining our sales presentation and value proposition to give the customer what they wanted and also to determine which level of support was required by each customer.

While many investors have observed that our revenue in 2025 remained relatively flat, our learning experience was a critical step at that time and serves as an important foundation for us to determine the course for our sales team to efficiently target the market, for our R&D team to build the right products and for our support team to be well equipped to onboard our customers. At the end of 2025, we had accomplished 2 key tasks: first, financial independence; and second, a market understanding of our customers and our value proposition.

In 2026, with a better understanding of our customer base, our product mix and how we can best serve our customer, we set out to validate our go-to-market strategy, reaching customers via distribution. One of the things we learned in 2025 and before was that in the laboratory space, getting in front of the customer and meeting the right decision-makers is really difficult. And post-COVID, if you didn't have a personal relationship, it was near impossible. We also learned that once we were in front of the decision-maker, we were quite successful in making the sale. So how do we get that door open for us? The distributors hold an important role in this field.

Working with the top 4 distributors in the industry, Thermo Fisher, Medline, McKesson and Cardinal Health, we have learned the power of the 200-plus sales reps each of the distributors employ. These are armies of well-trained, experienced and well-connected reps that have a long-established relationship with their customer, often spanning 10 to 15 years. There is no amount of money that would enable us to replicate even a fraction of that sales force power. And so we decided that distribution was the way to go. We also learned that each distributor is different, with different organizational structures, divisional responsibilities between different reps and organizational culture differences that dictate how best to interact with each distributor.

In 2026, we set out to figure the recipe for success with each distributor. During this process, we also learned what were the internal skill sets we needed to develop within our commercial team to best apply each recipe with each distributor. As we stand now at the end of 2026, we feel we figured out most of what we set out to discover in terms of the recipe with each distributor. That has led to some new hires in our commercial team and to a clear internal articulation of our go-to-market strategy via distribution. You've seen the gradual growth of the product division over the first 3 quarters of this year.

While it's always nice to see the business grow, this is by no means satisfactory to us nor it is a reflection of our planned growth trajectory going forward, quite the contrary. Precipio will -- 2027 will mark an important next phase in Precipio's evolution as we shift our focus from developing and validating our commercial strategy to accelerated growth. With the right products, a clear understanding of our target customers and established distribution strategy and the commercial infrastructure we're putting in place, we believe we now have the foundation to pursue a significantly higher rate of growth in our products business.

For the first time, we'd like to share with shareholders some specific financial objectives against which we intend to measure our progress. For our product division, we are targeting an annual revenue run rate exceeding $10 million by the end of 2027 compared with approximately $4 million annualized run rate based on our third quarter results of 2026. Our pathology business will also remain an important part of our growth strategy. Beyond its role in supporting product development and clinical validation, it also continues to generate the majority of our operating cash flow. We intend to continue growing this business, targeting an annualized revenue run rate of approximately $30 million by the end of 2027.

Together, these objectives represent a combined annualized revenue run rate exceeding $40 million by the end of 2027. To be clear, these are targets for the annualized revenue run rate we aim to achieve as we exit 2027 rather than a forecast of total revenue recognized during the year. We believe achieving these objectives would represent a significant milestone for Precipio, demonstrating the scalability of our products business while strengthening the financial foundation that enables us to fund continuing growth, product innovation and expansion into new diagnostic markets.

We recognize that these are ambitious objectives and delivering against them will require disciplined execution, but we believe the progress made over the past 2 years positions us well for this next phase of growth. Now let's turn to a review of Q3. Total revenue increased from approximately $7 million in Q2 to $7.3 million in Q3. Pathology revenue was approximately $6.3 million and product revenue exceeded, for the first time, $1 million a quarter, an exciting milestone. Adjusted EBITDA was approximately $400,000, consistent with Q2. Our operating cash flow was approximately $600,000 compared with approximately $700,000 in the second quarter.

Total cash increased by approximately $0.5 million during Q3, bringing our quarter end cash balance above $3.5 million compared with approximately $2.3 million a year earlier. These results give us a stronger financial foundation. With the confidence of a consistently cash-flowing business, it's now time to shift the balance. While maintaining positive cash flow, we plan to shift our focus to significant accelerated revenue growth. So let's discuss how we plan to scale up for growth on the product side. 2026 is all about understanding the recipe for growth.

As we discussed, we view distribution as the key source of scalability for our products business, and we wanted to understand how to best make that channel work before committing resources to a broader commercial expansion. We deliberately approached this with a relatively small commercial team and a measured level of spending. We wanted to refine the distributor model and our overall sales strategy before building a larger sales and marketing effort around them. The sequence was intentional: establish the approach, learn from execution and then invest in scaling it. We now believe we have a much clearer understanding of that recipe and how to support it.

Our ability to connect effectively with the distributor reps, arm them with information to get us a meeting and proceed to build a pipeline, all give us confidence we're ready for the next stage. It's now time to shift our emphasis from developing the model and understanding the recipe to implementing and expanding its reach. In 2027, growth will be our central commercial priority. We intend to significantly expand the commercial team and set aggressive goals for them while increasing marketing and technical support behind our products. It's time to pour gas on the fire, utilizing the incoming cash flow as resources towards accelerating the distributor and sales approach we spent this year developing.

An important part of that plan is bringing in a senior marketing executive to lead initiatives that were not previously pursued at this level. We want a more active presence in the market and a more systemic way to build awareness, credibility and access to prospective customers. That includes a stronger presence at relevant conferences, where we can engage laboratories, clinicians and our distribution partners. It also includes building a network of key opinion leaders who can provide clinical insights and help inform the evidence needed to support adoption. We plan to build clinical credibility through additional publications and case studies that explain the application and value of our technologies.

Our products need to be supported with evidence useful to the physicians and laboratories making testing decisions. Marketing will also work closely with sales on prospecting and customer access. The goal is to identify the right accounts, reach the people involved in testing decisions and give our sales team stronger materials and more opportunities to substantive customer discussions. That should extend to our distributors as well as to our direct commercial efforts. These initiatives are intended to work together. Conferences create opportunities for engagements, clinical relationships and evidence, strengthen our credibility and coordinated marketing and sales follow-up help move that interest towards evaluation and adoption.

Since quarter end, we have made changes to the commercial leadership and are bringing our products and pathology sales efforts under a more coordinated structure. Our recent product training week brought commercial, clinical and operational teams together to deepen product knowledge and strengthen customer conversations. These steps all support the broader growth effort we are preparing for next year. We will measure progress through customers completing implementation, beginning clinical use and placing repeat orders, ultimately resulting in revenue growth. Aggressive goals need to translate into results, and we intend to maintain that discipline and focus as we expand our commercial activity.

As we move from developing our commercial strategy to executing against a much more ambitious growth plan, operational leadership and accountability across the entire organization will become increasingly important. Zaki has been instrumental in building the infrastructure that brought us to this point. So now I've asked him to join this call and share his perspective on how we plan to scale the business from here. Zaki, all yours.

Ahmed Sabet: Thank you, Ilan, and good afternoon, everyone. As Ilan has outlined, we've spent the last several years building the foundation for Precipio's next stage of growth. My focus has been on developing an organization that not only can deliver high-quality diagnostic services and products, but to do so efficiently, profitably and at a significantly greater scale than where we operate today. I believe one of Precipio's greatest strengths is the operational infrastructure we've already built, and the opportunity we now have to leverage that infrastructure as the business grows. Within our pathology division, we've demonstrated our ability to grow revenue while improving efficiency and profitability.

We've invested in our people, systems, processes and laboratory capabilities, creating an operating model that we believe can support substantial additional volume without requiring a corresponding increase in our cost base. On the product side, we applied that same philosophy. We've built manufacturing capabilities, quality systems and technical support infrastructure designed not just for our current level of sales, but for the much larger business we intend to build. And importantly, these 2 divisions are deeply connected. Our clinical laboratory is not simply a source of revenue and cash flow.

It is also where we develop, validate and continuously improve our technologies, giving us a unique understanding of how our products perform in real-world clinical environments, and what our customers need to implement them successfully. To put the scale of the opportunity into perspective, we estimate that our existing operational infrastructure has the capacity to support approximately $100 million in annual revenue, roughly equally divided between pathology services and product manufacturing without requiring significant additional capital investment in our core facilities and equipment. That is a substantial amount of capacity relative to where our business stands today, and it creates an important opportunity for us to scale revenue, improve margins and drive greater profitability as we grow.

Ilan Danieli: Thank you, Zaki. In summary, the progression is clear. In 2025, we focused on reaching positive cash flow and financial independence. In 2026, as we generated cash, we studied and refined the commercial approach we believed can scale our products business. In 2027, we intend to put significant resources directly towards implementing that commercial approach and focus entirely on growth. We enter the next year with a strong financial foundation and a clear commercial direction. Our task is now to turn that preparation into faster growth. I'd like to thank our dedicated team of employees for their work and to our shareholders for your continued support. 2027 is going to be another pivotal year for us.

Zaki and I will now take your questions. Thank you.

Operator: [Operator Instructions] And your first question comes from the line of Sean Westropp with Deep Sail Capital.

Sean Westropp: Can you guys hear me okay?

Sean Westropp: All right. Great. Good quarter. I wanted to ask a little bit about the product sales and the scalability. You talked a lot about it in your comments here. When -- can you update us real quick on the current sales force, like what the size is and kind of like what -- how many folks you have in there? And then what -- you talked about reinvesting some of the cash flow into that organization. What, kind of, do you see that size in the next year or so?

Ilan Danieli: Yes. Thank you. Great question. Currently, our sales force is 4, and we are planning on doubling that next year. As I said in the remarks, now that we have the recipe, we know how to work with distributors and how to efficiently get from lead to customer to convert, this is the time to really scale it up. So we're going to expand that significantly. We expect by the beginning of the year to hire probably 2 more folks at least, and then continue throughout the year to really build this up.

Part of it is also to meet the demand from our distributors as we strengthen our connections with them, we'll get more motivated, more and more prospects, more and more meetings that we need to handle.

Sean Westropp: Got it. Great. And then on that sales cycle and sales side, do you have any idea now that you've kind of got 4 in place around ramp-up time of these new folks? When do they start kind of ramping up to actually able to deliver some product sales?

Ilan Danieli: Yes. That's -- unfortunately, that's still an unknown variable which should be broad range. Just case in point, we have a customer going live this quarter in Q4 that we probably were working on for 1.5 years almost. On the other side, we had a customer that we met for the first time in late September. And in fact, this week, they're going through training and they're going to start the validation, they'll probably go live before the end of the year. So I think the 2 bookends of customer onboarding time line is probably somewhere between 3 months and 18 months.

We have come up with a way to shorten that, and we're implementing that, but some customers trust the process [indiscernible] unfortunately. Now I think the way to fix that in terms of scaling up revenue is just to have a large N numbers. So every quarter, we've got another $0.25 million, $0.5 million of new revenue coming in, and that just -- it's just shots on goal at the end of the day.

Sean Westropp: Right, right. Great. And yes, on the gross margin side, the product gross margin, no changes there. I don't think you guys have always had pretty healthy gross margins on that. Is there anything on the distributor impacts that would affect the gross margin or anything like that?

Ilan Danieli: No, no, not at all. That's baked into calculation. So we're currently hovering around the kind of high 40s, 50% gross margin. As we scale up, when we double our revenue, I think -- I'm trying to do the math in my head, but I think the margins jump to probably the mid-60s and we'll continue that way. So this will, at a higher scale, it would be a good 70%, 75% gross margin.

Operator: And your next question comes from the line of Jack Holden with Kestrel.

Jack Holden: Congrats on the great quarter here and the profit growth. In Q2, you talked about the 25-plus new qualified customers. I was wondering if you could give any color on if any of those have converted and what kind of that current count is?

Ilan Danieli: In Q2, I'm trying to think probably -- I think we have in this quarter, maybe 2 or 3 of them go live and a whole bunch slotted during the first half of 2027. That's approximately the time line. There'll be some -- the drag later is than that. But we are seeing some good conversions and good progress on all of them as they go through the onboarding [indiscernible]

Jack Holden: Great. And then the $1 million product revenue, I noticed in the footnote something about some project revenue in there. Is that kind of a good baseline for us to work off of with kind of sequential quarterly growth as we exit into $10 million plus [indiscernible] 2027?

So we expect -- it's proven to be true that for the most part, they're going to have at least that in sequential quarters. What contributes to growth from the specific customers is when they add additional panels. And usually, a customer will start with 1 or 2 panels. And within 6 to 12 months, they'll have 3 to 4 panels. So we'll see kind of organic growth within those customers as well in the revenue growth.

But yes, I think our numbers have shown we had, I think, only once where the revenue has dropped, and that was because of the shift of an order from one quarter to the other.

Operator: And the next question comes from the line of [ Ben Zara ] with [ Tenet Capital ].

Ilan Danieli: [ Vincent ], thank you for your question. So no, there are no price declines or drops in demand. I think if you compare this to any other company, having a sales force of 3 or 4 is tiny. And we did that by design.

We could have easily raised $10 million in capital and hired 25 sales reps. And there's companies that do that. At the end of the day, every sales rep has an ROI on their back, if you will. And we want to make sure that we hit that.

And we've also had experience [ in the past ] where that hasn't happened. So yes, I understand. Your point is well taken, and we certainly are not happy with the sales growth. But I think as a company trying to balance shareholder value through dilution of additional capital versus growth, we made the decision to take this year to really study that. And next year, now that we have the cash reserves and we don't have to raise $10 million and dilute shareholders, we can do this properly. Does that answer your question?

Unknown Analyst: Not exactly. So -- partially. Ilan Danieli: Well, I see your point. I think you have to take into account the time line of results. So if you think about our sales team that was hired at the beginning of the year, by the time they get their training groups and are ready to go and really start to be impactful, that's middle of 2026, which means it's unlikely that they'll even see revenue coming from the efforts until the beginning of 2027. So by that logic, hiring people throughout 2027 will yield results in 2028.

But the goal is to kind of increase the level of the rate of growth.

But with our current pipeline, and that's why we have the confidence to kind of get to the first time the, sort of, guidance number, we believe we're going to get there.

And obviously, our sales team isn't just sitting around, that pipeline continues to grow. So I think we're pretty confident that we can beat the numbers that we've provided and kind of throughout the year, see a gradual acceleration to reaching that run rate.

Unknown Analyst: That's awesome. It sounds like a substantially larger pipeline than you've had in the past if half of it gets you to that run rate. Ilan Danieli: Yes, it's a little bit of both. So obviously, our sales team does not sit quietly and kind of [indiscernible] them. Unknown Analyst: Great. And just one more for me. We're probably going to hire 1 or 2 more reps on the pathology side as well. And I think ultimately, [indiscernible] management retention.

We've been really focused this year on the product side and all the things we talked about, figuring out the recipe, really building a strong team, building the marketing backbone [indiscernible] for this. There's not really any change to any products. The services side is pretty standard in terms of the analysis we do for patient samples that come in. So that stays the same. Hopefully, that answers your question.

#3176. Reddit Reviews goes against the whole philosophy of the platform, say users

Many Redditors have expressed dismay at the launch of Reddit Reviews, a new AI-powered feature which aims to summarise posts about particular products.

Reddit is positioning the feature as a way to save time and effort when researching a potential purchase, but many Redditors say that replacing human interaction with AI summaries is antithetical to the whole philosophy of the platform – and is going to make the existing spam problem massively worse …

The value of customer reviews on ecommerce platforms like Amazon is becoming increasingly questionable thanks to practices like astroturfing by brands and offering people free products in return for five-star reviews.

That’s led to Reddit becoming one of the most trusted sources of feedback and advice on potential purchases, precisely because it’s a forum in which real people are free to express their true opinions. Indeed, many use a filter in their Google searches to draw content from Reddit specifically, adding the suffix ‘site:reddit.com’.

Reddit certainly isn’t immune to astroturfing – that is, fake posts by brands posing as ordinary users – but moderators put a lot of work into deleting spam and other inauthentic posts.

The platform yesterday announced the launch of Reddit Reviews, in which AI summarises the posts made about particular products and product categories. It’s being pitched as a way for people to save time when seeking the product opinions of Redditors.

Across Reddit’s communities, people discuss everything from hobbies and daily life to products they’re researching. By offering perspectives grounded in real experience, these conversations provide valuable context in every purchase decision journey […]

Today, we are starting to test Reddit Reviews, a new experience that organizes product conversations from across Reddit into dedicated reviews and highlights the most important takeaways from across our communities.

However, as CNET spotted, the move has led to a backlash by many Redditors and subreddit moderators.

“I’ve already seen this in practice and it is a nightmare. It turns a basic conversation into an ad-ridden distracting mess. It’s horrible to read and had me fleeing every thread I saw it in.”

“I am a moderator on a couple of health subs and we explicitly do not allow advertisements because most of them are bullshit slop and completely predatory for vulnerable and newly diagnosed patients. We do not want, or need this, on our subs!”

“Yeah, this definitely isn’t going to lead to even more fake account stealth marketing efforts across the site.”

“This is going to make our spam fighting even worse. This is horrible.”

“Every decision made by Reddit lately encourages spam and/or abuse that will make spam.”

“Not a single person who uses Reddit wants this.”

“You are incentivising existing spammers to continue or step up their activities, now that there’s a new well they can poison.”

I find it hard to disagree with the view that almost every monetization step the platform has made has degraded the user experience. This seems almost guaranteed to be another one.

Apple vs Google vs Samsung in a smartwatch showdown

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

I’ve spent the past few months diving deep into the new Apple Watch Series 12, Google Pixel Watch 5, and Samsung Galaxy Watch 9. In fact, I wrote long-form reviews of the latter two and have tested the former head-to-head against the competition over a dozen times.

Hi, I’m Dan, and I lead our smartwatch coverage here at Tom’s Guide, and I often get asked, “OS preference aside, which smartwatch from the BIG THREE would I actually buy in 2026?”

It’s a difficult question to answer, given that all three models have advantages over their competitors. Moreover, Apple, Google, and Samsung all make seriously lovely wearables — some of the best smartwatches in 2026 — brimming with smart, health, safety, and connectivity features.

But enough excuses. Below, I’ve compared the Apple Watch 12, Pixel Watch 5, and Galaxy Watch 9 across six categories — cost, design, display, fitness/recovery features, health/safety features, and battery — with a winner or winners declared for each. If you’re short on time, you can find my ultimate verdict at the very end.

The Apple Watch Series 12 (42mm) and Pixel Watch 5 (41mm) each start at $399 for the smaller respective models without cellular. (Note: The Pixel Watch 5 is currently $100 off at Amazon.) The Galaxy Watch 9 (40mm) is a tiny bit cheaper, starting at $379.

If you spring for the larger size with cellular connectivity, the Apple Watch Series 12 (46mm) is the priciest at $549, followed by the Pixel Watch 5 (45mm) at $529, with the Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 (44mm) being the best bargain of the fully-loaded big boys at $459.

Based on value alone, Samsung wins this category; however, a savings of $20 to $100 is unlikely to be the determining factor in which smartwatch I’d ultimately buy. Moreover, I prefer smaller watches and don't really need cellular, diminishing Samsung’s pricing advantage.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The Apple Watch Series 12, Google Pixel Watch 5, and Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 are all extremely well-built, durable, and comfortable devices based on my extended testing. Each boasts 50 meters of water resistance, enough for surface-level swims, with metal cases and scratch-resistant displays.

No matter which model you go with, you get two physical controls along the side of the case. On the Galaxy Watch 9, those controls come in the form of two identical-looking buttons. On the Pixel Watch 5 and Apple Watch 12, you get a physical button and a digital crown that can be both turned and pressed, making it more valuable than a standard button.

As a result, I prefer the controls of the latest Apple Watch and Pixel Watch to those of the newest Galaxy Watch.

Each of the major manufacturers has settled on a unique case shape. Apple is a square, Google is a circle, and Samsung is a squarish circle.

In 2026, each of the major full-featured smartwatch manufacturers has settled on a unique case shape. Apple is a square, Google is a circle, and Samsung is a squarish circle. Of the three shapes, I prefer Apple’s the best.

The Galaxy Watch 9’s circular display mounted on a rounded square case results in what feels like wasted space around the bezel. Meanwhile, the Pixel Watch 5’s circular case coupled with its domed Actua 360 circular display makes the watch feel a little too bubbly/sit rather high on my wrist.

With the best controls and sleekest case design, Apple gets my nod in this category.

All three of these smartwatches sport bright, crisp, and well-saturated AMOLED screens. However, Samsung and Google’s displays offer a higher maximum output (they get brighter) than Apple’s, making them a bit easier to read in direct sunlight.

The latest Apple Watch Series 12 screen maxes out at 2,000 nits compared to 3,000 nits for the Galaxy Watch 9 and Pixel Watch 5.

Winner: Google Pixel Watch 5 and Samsung Galaxy Watch 9

I’ve spent a ton of time exploring the vast array of fitness tracking and workout planning features found in the best smartwatch models of 2026. That said, for basic insights into your physical activity, sleep quality, and overall well-being, the Apple Watch 12, Pixel Watch 5, or Samsung Galaxy Watch 9 will all serve you well.

However, for more advanced workout training and recovery insights that don’t require a subscription, Samsung has both Apple and Google beat. Don’t get me wrong, the new Google Health app (formerly the Fitbit app) is jam-packed with features comparable to what the Samsung Health app offers. However, the best ones require a monthly Google Health Premium subscription ($9.99 a month or $99 for the year). That’s not the case for the Galaxy Watch.

Samsung’s free daily sleep reports are also the most comprehensive of the three, [and] only the Galaxy Watch 9 and Apple Watch 12 offer FDA-cleared sleep apnea detection.

Samsung’s free daily sleep reports are also the most comprehensive of the three, in my opinion. Also, only the Galaxy Watch 9 and Apple Watch 12 offer FDA-cleared sleep apnea detection.

Apple’s health and fitness tracking chops are decent, but I still feel the Cupertino Kid is catching up to its two biggest competitors when it comes to dynamic wellness insights. For example, Apple just got a daily readiness score this year. Samsung, meanwhile, has offered an “Energy Score” since 2024, right around the same time Google launched its daily readiness score.

Apple’s sleep score feature is also relatively new (launched in 2025), and from my experience, it tends to be the most optimistic of the three, which is either a good thing or a bad thing, depending on how you look at it.

All three smartwatches have some form of fall/crash detection, which can automatically call for help when triggered, as well as user-activated SOS safety tools. You also get alerts for high/low heart rates, along with AFib detection and SpO2 readings.

However, only the Apple Watch 12 offers 24-7 hypertension alerts, designed to detect signs of high blood pressure early. On the other hand, only the Pixel Watch 5 offers Loss of Pulse Detection and Breathing Emergency Detection, both of which work similarly to fall/crash detection.

The Pixel Watch 5 also supports new Blood Pressure Trends and Insulin Resistance Trends, along with Breathing Quality Trends, making it arguably the king of on-wrist health and safety in 2026.

On paper, the Apple Watch 12 is supposed to last up to 24 hours per charge, while the Galaxy Watch 9 and Pixel Watch 5 are rated at up to 40 hours per charge. In reality, both the Apple Watch and Galaxy Watch easily meet their battery life ratings.

The Pixel Watch 5, meanwhile, far surpasses the 40-hour rating in my testing. I reviewed the larger model and averaged closer to 48 hours per charge.

Ultimately, if I were spending my hard-earned money on one of the top smartwatches in 2026 — ignoring smartphone OS preferences — I’d likely choose the Apple Watch Series 12 over the Google Pixel Watch 5 or Samsung Galaxy Watch 9.

The main reason is that I prefer the design of the Apple Watch Series 12 to the competition. I also genuinely appreciate Apple’s simple approach to daily fitness and health tracking — via “closing your rings” — even if it's a little bit basic for hardcore users.

I prefer the design of the Apple Watch Series 12 to the competition. I also genuinely appreciate Apple’s simple approach to daily fitness and health tracking.

Apple is still playing catch-up a bit when it comes to health and advanced training metrics, but the brand has definitely made up for lost ground in 2026 with the debut of a daily readiness score, heart rate variability tracking, the forthcoming health age metric, and a greater overall emphasis on tracking long-term wellness trends.

Still, Google has Apple beat when it comes to on-wrist safety, and Samsung’s health/fitness tools remain a bit more comprehensive than Apple’s... for now. All that said, I really wish Apple would step up its game when it comes to battery performance.

#3172. Can Cathie Wood's Ark Invest ETF Make a Comeback With Its Large SpaceX Position?

SpaceX will make the Ark Innovation ETF more volatile, and AI trends ultimately determine the fund's fate.

Discussions about Cathie Wood being a better investor than Warren Buffett feel like a distant memory. Still, her flagship Ark Innovation ETF (ARKK -2.38%) has produced an annualized 15.5% return over the past decade. However, that also includes an annualized 9.1% loss over the past five years, showing the volatile nature of the fund.

Consistent with high volatility, she has quickly turned Space Exploration Technologies (SPCX +0.72%) into her second-largest holding, behind only Tesla (TSLA +0.46%). Elon Musk has a big say in how Wood's fund performs, but is that the right move? Here's what investors should consider.

Ark Invest CEO Cathie Wood. Image source: Getty Images.

You won't find the slightest bit of value investing in Wood's portfolio, unless you count Nvidia (NVDA -5.47%) as a value stock. While that's a fair argument due to its relatively low P/E ratio, it's hard to call companies like Coinbase (COIN -2.92%), Tempus AI (TEM -4.62%), and OpenAI value stocks. These three companies make up the fund's top 10 holdings, and they are extremely volatile.

Consistent with its annualized five- and 10-year returns, investors can expect a volatile ride with dramatic price action. SpaceX fits the mold, with many 10% upswings and downswings since its June IPO.

A 0.75% expense ratio certainly works against the fund's desirability, but it is well positioned for the most high-risk, high-reward AI opportunities.

A $1.8 trillion market cap implies a lofty valuation and may limit future growth opportunities compared to smaller AI stocks. However, the business is undeniably growing at a rapid pace. Revenue surged by 161% year over year, with net operating income of $2.8 billion as a major highlight.

The super intelligence segment is doing the heavy lifting. That part of the business grew by 830% year over year to $7.56 billion. Growth almost tripled sequentially. Space revenue was also up 84% sequentially, showing that it's not just an AI data center stock. For now, though, AI is still firmly in the driver's seat of SpaceX's future growth.

The primary concern is whether most of future growth is already priced in at a $1.8 trillion market cap. However, SpaceX's earnings results and Musk's desire to have up to 20 gigawatts of power by the end of 2027 suggest that more gains are possible. Granted, Musk will have to achieve that 20-gigawatt total, which may be more difficult due to midterm election results.

Ark Innovation holders should watch closely for any AI developments. The tone of the industry will directly impact Wood's fund in a meaningful way since it is heavily exposed to the industry. However, a 0.75% expense ratio is a bit too high for me.

#3171. Claude’s new Personal Finance tool aims to help analyze your spending – read-only, of course

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Anthropic has released what appears to be its answer to ChatGPT Finances.

You can now share your financial information with Claude and ask the chatbot for insights on your spending.

Also: Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info

Personal Finance in Claude, which Anthropic announced Thursday, reviews your connected accounts through read-only access via Plaid. That security measure follows OpenAI’s equivalent feature, ChatGPT Finances, which launched in May. Here’s what to know.

Functionally, this feature appears similar to ChatGPT Finances: It lets you link as many bank and credit card accounts as you’d like to Claude via Plaid with read-only access. You can then ask Claude where you spent your money this month or whether you can afford to take a vacation in six months, for example.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

Also: Stop sharing your passwords with AI agents

According to Anthropic, the feature is a response to existing use patterns: the company’s April usage report found that financial advice was one of the main topics users ask Claude for help with.

“For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank’s name, each account’s name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren’t used to train our models.”

The idea behind the feature is that you can ask follow-up questions and request more insights about spending habits, trends over time, and future goals based on what Claude finds, similar to any other Claude conversation. The tool will also generate tables and charts to visualize your financial information.

“You can ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what’s due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds it as an artifact you can keep adjusting and coming back to,” an Anthropic representative told ZDNET via email.

Also: I connected ChatGPT to my bank, and it’s my go-to finance app now

You can also expect an ad-free experience in the feature.

“Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer,” the company said in the announcement.

The company added that because Claude is using actual transaction data and not memory, the feature shouldn’t hallucinate.

“It can list the exact transactions behind any number so you can check its math,” Anthropic said via email. “Like any AI, it can make mistakes, so for anything important, we recommend confirming with your bank.”

Still, the difference — and for many, the appeal — here is the natural language interface. Other finance apps don’t necessarily have an easy, accessible chat function where users can shoot off quick questions like they would to a human financial planner. These assistants also present historical budget analysis in plain English, rather than requiring users to interpret dashboards themselves, which users may see as a perk.

Also: 5 ways to use AI when your budget is tight

On Reddit, many users find ChatGPT Finances to be accurate and reliable. One Reddit user said ChatGPT Finance seemed to have Mint or Monarch potential, but noted it was still “weaker” than those apps in some areas, such as historical syncing, high-quality dashboards, and generating full statement PDFs.

“ChatGPT has genuinely helped me make better financial decisions,” she wrote.

Anthropic noted that users shouldn’t look to Personal Finance for Claude as a total authority. “Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust,” the company said in the announcement.

“We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it” — indicating a more integrated financial planning system within Claude may be on the way.

#3170. This video lets you actually see the ‘incredible’ new MacBook Pro cooling system

When Apple launched the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display, the company said that it had completely redesigned the cooling system for “incredible sustained performance.”

That could sound like marketing hype, but a YouTuber has found a great way to let us actually see the new system living up to Apple’s claims …

The real-life performance of any electronic device depends not only on the power of the chip but a range of additional factors. A key one is the effectiveness of the cooling system, because when the device gets too hot, the performance will be throttled in order to avoid damage.

In the worst of cases, the theoretical maximum performance of a chip is only delivered for a very short time before it is throttled back to a much lower level. Thermal management is absolutely key in the case of a laptop like the MacBook Pro.

Apple said that the latest model has a completely new cooling system.

A completely redesigned thermal architecture enables […] incredible sustained performance of M5 Pro and M5 Max, even in a lighter design, while redirecting warm air away from the display.

As Macworld spotted, a YouTuber has found a simple but clever way to enable us to actually see the difference with our own eyes.

A YouTube video by Geekerwan compared the mini-LED MacBook Pro with the new PROLED XDR model using a fog machine. With each MacBook’s fans running, you can clearly see how the internal design disperses the heat: In the old model, heat goes both out and up through the display, while the PROLED pushes the heat toward the back of the device through the hinge.

Cooling is particularly challenging when the laptop is closed while connected to an external monitor, and the results of the testing show a dramatic improvement by the latest model. You can watch the video below, which links directly to the demo – but Geekerwan’s videos are always worth watching in full, so click here to watch the whole thing.
